[CHAPTER 28:	GLOSSARY	28\-1](#_bookmark301)

title: Introduction
text:
The first step in determining the acceptability of title to a particular parcel of real property is to conduct or request a “*title search*\.” A title search involves a search of the Public Records, usually by an experienced abstractor or attorney, for all of the instruments of record in the chain of title during a specified time period that may affect title to the subject property\.

An “*abstract of title*” is a condensed summary of conveyances and other matters found in the Public Records which affect title to the subject property\. An abstract is compiled from a title search covering a particular time period\. The notes made in the field by an abstractor are sometimes referred to as a “*run sheet*\.”

An abstract should note all recorded documents that affect title to the subject property that have not been barred or cancelled of record, such as \(a\) the original land patent, \(b\) deeds, \(c\) deeds of trust, \(d\) reservations, \(e\) chancery proceedings, such as a will probate or estate administration, \(f\) easements, covenants, conditions, and restrictions, \(g\) tax assessments, payments, and sales, and \(h\) notices of lien filings, such as *lis pendens*, construction liens, materialman liens, federal tax liens, and judgments\. An abstract should also contain copies of the particular township plat and governmental survey obtained from the clerk’s office\. A thorough abstract will contain a summary of these records arranged in chronological order, showing the record ownership of the subject property over a period of time\. This chronological summary is referred to as a “*chain of title*\.*” *Through a chain of title, the ownership of the subject property can be traced from a “*base*” or “*root” *title to its present owner\.

If an abstractor or an affiliate of the Company \(e\.g\., First American Abstract Company\) conducts the title search, the results of the title search are generally provided in the form of a “*title search report*\.” As with abstracts, title search reports may be limited in scope to cover only a particular search period or may be a complete search of the record—going back to the original land patent\. In order to insure mineral or other subsurface rights, a complete search back to the original land patent by a professional Landman is required\. A title search report provides a concise summary all the title search information along with copies of documents in order for the Issuing Agent to evaluate and determine the insurability of title\.

The next step, *“title examination,” *involves a thorough review of the title search report and any supporting documentation provided with the report to determine the legal sufficiency of the instruments found in the chain of title, their relative effect on title, and whether any title defects exist\. Should a title examination reveal a title defect, curative work may be necessary to clear the defect\. Examples of defects requiring curative work are unpaid taxes, unsatisfied mortgages, judgments against the seller, and restrictions limiting the use of the land\.

title: Preliminary Information
Search Periods
text:
Mississippi does not currently have a Marketable Record Title Act and there is no statute regarding the minimum search period\. Instead, the standard for conducting title searches in Mississippi has evolved over time by custom\.

For residential transactions, title searches cover a minimum search period of 32 years\. This 32\-year search period is derived from 21 years of minority, the 10\-year period of adverse possession, and a possible one\-year gestation period\. See Miss\. Code Ann\. §§ 1\-3\-27, 15\-1\-13\. For commercial transactions, title searches cover a minimum search period of 50 years\. Finally, a search all the way back to the original federal land patent is required for searches involving mineral interests\. Below is a search period chart:

title: Examination of the Record – Chancery Clerk’s Office
parent_hierarchy: Examination of the Record – Chancery Clerk’s Office
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-9 - Examination of the Record – Chancery Clerk’s Office
text: In Mississippi, chancery courts are courts of equity and have full jurisdiction in “\(a\) all matters in equity, \(b\) divorce and alimony, \(c\) matters testamentary and of administration, \(d\) minors’ business, \(e\) \[matters involving competence of a person\], and \(f\) all cases in which the court had jurisdiction under the laws in force when this constitution \[was\] put in operation\.” Miss\. Const\. art\. VI, § 159 \(1890\)\. Chancery courts also have jurisdiction in suits to try title, to cancel deeds and other clouds upon title to real estate, to decree or displace possession, and to decree rents and compensation for improvements and taxes\. Miss\. Const\. art\. VI, § 160 \(1890\)\. As such, the chancery clerk’s office maintains records relating to patents, deeds, mortgages, deeds of trust, assignments, liens, *lis pendens *notices, probate records, and other court files affecting title to lands\.

title: Book of original entries
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-10 - Book of original entries
text: Mississippi is a “*public lands*” state\. All public lands in the state, upon admission to the union, belonged to the United States\. Only title to tidelands and navigable waters were granted to the state, subject to the public trust\. Cinque Bambini Partn\. v\. State, 491 So\.2d 508 \(Miss\. 1986\)\. Until lands are patented, title remains in the United States\. Best v\. Humboldt Placer Min\. Co\., 371 U\.S\. 334, 336 \(1963\)\. Therefore, an Issuing Agent must begin his title examination by confirming that a land patent has been issued by the United States and has been properly executed and recorded\. If no patent is recorded, the Bureau of Land Management should be contacted to confirm whether one has been issued and to secure a copy\.

title: General and sectional indices
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-11 - General and sectional indices
text:
After verifying the patent, the next step in the title examination procedure is to conduct a thorough search of both the general and sectional indices, which are maintained by the office of the chancery clerk in the county in which the subject property is located\.

The chancery clerk is required to maintain three *general indices*: one for deeds, one for deeds of trust and mortgages, and one for general substitutions of trustees\. Miss\. Code Ann\. §§ 89\-5\-33\(1\), 89\-5\-29, 89\-5\-45\. Each general index book is assigned a letter of the alphabet and each instrument is indexed by the first letter of the last name of parties to the instrument\. When an instrument is recorded, the clerk will place the name of the grantor on the appropriate page of the direct \(or “grantor”\) general index, and will include the name of the grantee, date, and other information\. By contrast, the reverse \(or “grantee”\) general index is arranged by the grantee’s name\.

The chancery clerk is also required to maintain a *sectional index *to instruments describing land which are also entered in a general index\. Miss\. Code Ann\. § 89\-5\-33\(2\)\. The sectional index contains the name of each maker of the instrument, the name of each person to whom made, the date, type of instrument, and the appropriate reference where recorded\. The sectional index must also set forth the location of the land described in the instrument by either \(a\) quarter section or governmental lot for each section, township and range established by governmental survey, or \(b\) by lot number for platted subdivisions, official surveys, and unofficial subdivisions\.

It is important to note that title examinations should never rely solely on the sectional index\. Sun Oil Co\. v\. Broadhead, 323 So\. 2d 95 \(Miss\. 1975\)\. Further, in the event of conflict between the general and the sectional indices, the notice imparted by the general index will prevail except to the extent the land is described by lot number for platted subdivisions, official surveys and unofficial subdivisions and surveys commonly in use, the sectional index will prevail\. Alamac LLC v\. Travelers Bank & Trust, FSB, 941 So\. 2d 219 \(Miss\. App\. 2006\)\.

Each county also keeps a book of general substitutions of trustees\. Miss\. Code Ann\. § 89\-5\-45\. In Mississippi, a general substitution of trustee can be made if the deed of trust beneficiary is \(a\) an agency of the state or federal government, \(b\) a national or state chartered bank or savings and loan institution, \(c\) a federal land bank, \(d\) a production credit association, or \(e\) an insurance company\. This book is arranged by beneficiary name, and will identify the substitute trustee for all mortgages or deeds of trust held by the beneficiary in the county\.

The act of recording an instrument is what constitutes constructive notice that the conveyance has occurred\. Miss\. Code Ann\. §§ 89\-5\-1, 89\-5\-3, 89\-5\-5; Sowell v\. Rankin, 82 So\. 317 \(Miss\. 1919\) \(“Constructive notice of the making of a deed begins the moment it is lodged with the proper officer for record”\)\. The recording party is not required to see that the conveyance is properly indexed, but may instead rely on the act of recording as notice\. Hilbun v\. Twin States Land & Timber Co*\.*, 1998 Miss\. App\. LEXIS 621 \(Miss\. Ct\. App\. July 28, 1998\) \(unpublished opinion\)\. As a side, the Mississippi Court of Appeals has recently held that filing in the wrong judicial district of a county is tantamount to filing in the wrong county and does not constitute constructive notice\. Harrison County Util\. Auth\. v\. Helen Peterson Walker, 143 So\. 3d 608, 613\-14 \(Miss\. App\. 2014\) \(citing Miss\. Code Ann\. §§ 89\-5\-1, 89\-5\-3, 89\-5\-41\)\.

title: Map and plat book
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-12 - Map and plat book
text: The chancery clerk is required to maintain a certified duplicate of each subdivision platmade of any city, town, or village, or addition thereto\. Miss\. Code Ann\. §§ 19\-27\-21 to 27\.

title: Lis pendens record
text:
When a plaintiff files suit in any court to enforce a lien upon, a right to, or an interest in any real estate, the plaintiff should file a notice with the chancery clerk containing the names of all the parties to the suit, a description of the real estate, and a brief statement of the nature of the lien, right, or interest sought to be enforced, unless the claim is founded upon a recorded instrument or judgment in the county in which the real estate is located\. Miss\. Code Ann\. § 11\-47\-3\. This notice, referred to as a “*lis pendens *notice”, serves to put the world on notice of the plaintiff’s claimed lien on or interest in the property\. The chancery

clerk will record this notice in the “*Lis Pendens *Record” and will index the notice in both a direct and reverse index, arranged by the name of each party to the litigation\. Miss\. Code Ann\. §§ 11\-47\-1, 11\-47\-7*\. *If a plaintiff fails to record the notice, the suit will not affect the rights of a bona fide purchaser or incumbrancer, unless they have actual notice of the suit\. Miss\. Code Ann\. § 11\-47\-9\. When the suit is concluded, the plaintiff should file a notice of the results with the clerk\. Miss\. Code Ann\. § 11\-47\-11\.

title: State tax liens
text:
Tax liens used to be filed in the circuit clerk’s office in the county in which the taxpayer resided or owned property and were enrolled on the judgment rolls of these counties\. Effective January 1, 2015, however, all tax liens are enrolled online on the State Tax Lien Registry, which is available at [www\.liens\.ms\.gov](http://www.liens.ms.gov/)\. Miss\. Code Ann\. § 85\-11\-19\. Older tax liens that were enrolled on the judgment rolls of the counties after January 1, 2008 and were not shown as “satisfied” or “issued in error” as of January 1, 2015, were immediately enrolled on the new State Tax Lien Registry\. Under Miss\. Code Ann\. § 27\-7\-55, notices of tax liens for income and franchise tax penalties and interest may also be filed with the circuit clerk on the judgment roll of the county in which the taxpayer resides or owns property\. However, such a filing would be in addition to \(not in lieu of\) filing on the registry\.

Unpaid state, county, and municipal *ad valorem *taxes are secured by a lien on the property assessed\. Miss\. Code Ann\. § 27\-35\-1\. Other taxes that could create a lien on real property include corporate franchise taxes, sales taxes, tobacco taxes, alcoholic beverage taxes, and estate taxes\. For the code provisions addressing these taxes and the lien period, *see *Miss\. Code Ann\. §§ 27\-71\-333 \(alcohol\), 27\-13\-29 \(corporate franchise\), 27\-9\-35 \(estate\), 27\-65\-57 \(sales\), 27\-69\-41 \(tobacco\)\.

title: Tax sales
text:
Each year, the tax collector sells land on which taxes have not been paid to the highest bidder for an amount equal to the taxes, damages, costs, and interest accrued to that date\. Miss\. Code Ann\. § 27\-41\-

59\. If no bids are received, the land is sold to the State of Mississippi\. *Id*\. If bids are received, the property is sold to the highest bidder\. In most counties, records of tax sales are shown on the sectional index\. In a few counties, they are separately indexed in a tax sale index\.

An owner of land sold for taxes, any other person with an interest in the land, or a person acting on the owner’s behalf and with the owner’s consent may redeem the land within two years from the date of the tax sale\. Miss\. Code Ann\. § 27\-45\-3\. If tax sale property is redeemed, the chancery clerk will execute a release of all claims or title that either the state or the tax sale purchaser may have\. *Id*\. The release is recorded and operates as a quitclaim on the part of the state or the tax sale purchaser\. *Id*\.

title: Federal liens
text:
“If any person liable to pay any \[federal\] tax neglects or refuses to pay the same after demand, the amount including \[interest, penalties, additional tax, and costs\] shall be a lien in favor of the United States upon all property and rights to property, whether real or personal, belonging to such person\.” 26 U\.S\.C\. § 6321\. If the taxpayer fails to pay or refuses to pay the tax assessed after receiving notice and demand, the government will file a notice of federal tax lien\.

Pursuant to Mississippi’s Uniform Federal Lien Registration Act, all notices of federal liens on real property must be filed in the chancery clerk’s office in the county where the real property is located\. Miss\. Code Ann\. § 85\-8\-5\. The notices of these liens, together with any certificates of release, nonattachment, discharge, or subordination, will be filed in an alphabetical lien index, arranged by the name of the person named in the notice\.

For liens on personal property, the notice is filed in either \(a\) chancery clerk’s office in the county where the owner resides at the time of lien filing; or \(b\) the office of the Secretary of State if the person

against whose interest the lien applies is \(i\) an entity taxed as corporation or partnership whose principal office is located in Mississippi, \(ii\) a trust, or \(iii\) the estate of a decedent\. *Id*\. Notices filed with the Secretary of State are indexed in the same manner as UCC financing statements\. Miss\. Code Ann\. §§ 85\-8\-9; 75\-9\-

519\. Certificates of release or nonattachment are indexed as if the certificate were a UCC termination statement\. Miss\. Code Ann\. § 85\-8\-9\(2\)\. Certificates of discharge or subordination are indexed as if the certificate were a release of collateral\. *Id*\. The Act does not apply to security interests governed by the provisions of the UCC—Secured Transactions\. Miss Code Ann\. § 85\-8\-3\.

title: Chancery docket
text: The chancery clerk is required to maintain a general index of all chancery court causes and probate court causes which have been finally disposed of in the courts of the county\. Miss\. Code Ann\. § 19\-15\-7\. In some counties, the chancery docket is divided into separate books\. The chancery docket lists the names of the complainants and defendants and will list matters involving incompetency, probate, minors, divorce, and eminent domain\. The names of all owners in the chain of title should be run against both the complainant and defendant sides of each index for their period of ownership plus a few years before and after their period of ownership\. In some cases, only the first one or two complainants are indexed\.

title: Notice of liens
text: Each chancery clerk is required to maintain, as a part of the land records of their county, a record entitled “Notice of Liens” wherein notices shall be filed and recorded\. Miss\. Code Ann\. § 85\-7\-131 \(oil and gas well construction\); Miss\. Code Ann\. § 85\-7\-133; Miss\. Code Ann § 85\-7\-401 \(special \[construction\] liens on real estate\); Miss\. Code Ann § 85\-7\-405\. Such liens shall not take effect until notation thereof is filed and recorded in the record showing a description of the property involved, the name of the lienors, the date of filing, if and where suit is filed, and if and where contract is filed or recorded\.

title: 1\.04\.10 Uniform commercial code
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-19 - 1\.04\.10 Uniform commercial code
text: Although financing statements are generally filed in the Office of the Secretary of State, to perfect a security interest or agricultural lien in \(i\) as\-extracted collateral or timber to be cut, or \(ii\) collateral that is or is to become a fixture, the financing statement must be filed of record in the chancery clerk’s office\. Miss\. Code Ann\. § 75\-9\-301 *et seq*\.

title: Examination of the Record – Circuit Clerk’s Office
parent_hierarchy: Examination of the Record – Circuit Clerk’s Office
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-20 - Examination of the Record – Circuit Clerk’s Office
text: Circuit courts, unlike chancery courts, are courts of general jurisdiction, which means that they have original jurisdiction in all civil and criminal matters that are not vested in some other court\. Miss\. Const\. art\. VI, § 156 \(1890\)\. The circuit clerk’s office maintains records relating to judgments \(the “judgment roll”\)\.

title: Judgment roll
text: A judgment constitutes a lien upon and binds all of a defendant’s property once that judgment is enrolled\. Miss\. Code Ann\. §§ 11\-7\-191, 11\-7\-197\. The chancery clerk must enroll judgments within 20 days after the end of each term of the circuit court\. Miss\. Code Ann\. § 11\-7\-189\. The judgment roll should be checked for at least the previous 10 years\.

title: Circuit and county dockets
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-22 - Circuit and county dockets
text: If a *lis pendens *notice is discovered in the chancery court search, then the circuit and county dockets should be searched to make sure there are no pending lawsuits against the current owner and no judgments have been rendered against parties in the chain of title\. The primary actions affecting real estate in the circuit court are suits in ejectment, injunctions, trespass, condemnation, and unlawful entry and detainer\.

title: Examination of the Record – Tax Collector’s Office
parent_hierarchy: Examination of the Record – Tax Collector’s Office
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-23 - Examination of the Record – Tax Collector’s Office
text: Although the tax collector is required to deliver a book of duplicate tax receipts for each prior year—which remains as a permanent record in the chancery clerk’s office—the current year’s receipts are maintained in the tax collector’s office\. Miss\. Code Ann\. § 27\-41\-43\. Therefore, taxes and special assessments for the current year must be examined in the tax collector’s office\.

title: Generally
text: Garbage in, garbage out \(GIGO\) in the field of computer science or information and communications technology refers to the fact that computers, since they operate by logical processes, will unquestioningly process flawed, even nonsensical, input data \(“*garbage in*”\) and produce undesired, often nonsensical, output \(“*garbage out*”\)\. In many ways, this principle applies to title search products\. More specifically, when a request for a search product is submitted, abstractors will complete the search based on the facts provided\. If a search is required on a particular property and the abstractor is only provided with a street address, then the abstractor will search for the parcel number associated with that street address and then search the legal description associated with that parcel number\. Without more details abstractors often have no way of determining whether or not the property described in the deed is actually the \(or all of the\) property that the Issuing Agent intended the search to cover\. For this reason, it is imperative that Issuing Agents provide sufficient information when requesting a search product\.

title: Information needed
text:
When submitting a request for a title search product, the following information should be provided:

- Requester Details
	- Agent’s name, file number, contact information and preferred delivery method
- Search Details
	- Search type – full search, update only, other
	- Search period – 32 years, 50 years, to patent, other
	- Search county and judicial district
	- Required Copies – Title chain only, vesting deed and pertinent pages, all easements, liens and encumbrances, other
	- Special instructions, if any
- Property Details
	- Property type – one\-to\-four single family residential or commercial/other
	- Estate or Interest – fee simple, leasehold, easement appurtenant, other
	- Owner’s name
	- Buyer’s name
	- Property address
	- Parcel number\(s\)
	- Legal description
- Signature

A sample form of request for a title search product is available in Section \.

title: Types of Title Search Products
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-27 - Types of Title Search Products
text: There are two types of search reports available through First American Abstract Company\. They are commonly referred to as a “*title search report*” and an “*owner’s and encumbrance report*\.”

title: Title search report \(full/update\)
text:
A title search report is usually requested for sale transactions and for transactions that involve construction loans\. A title search report provides a chain of title going back 32 years \(unless a longer search period is requested\), and it includes information related to: \(1\) open mortgages and deeds of trust, \(2\) judgments, \(3\) liens which may be attached to the property, \(4\) deeds for all current and prior owners during the search period, \(5\) easements, \(6\) covenants, conditions and restrictions, \(7\) agreements, resolutions, and ordinances, and \(8\) other matters of record that are filed in the public land records\.

The title search report is an “informational report” and is not an opinion, warranty, guarantee, or insurance\. Instead, it is simply a reflection of the public record as it stands on the date of the search\. However, a title search report can be used in conjunction with the issuance of a title insurance policy\.

title: Owner’s and encumbrance report; “current owner report”
parent_hierarchy: Owner’s and encumbrance report; “current owner report”
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-29 - Owner’s and encumbrance report; “current owner report”
text:
An owner’s and encumbrance report \(also called “O&E report” for short, or “current owner report”\) is a limited search report that identifies the last recorded owner of the property, the legal description of the property, and any open liens, mortgages, *lis pendens*, and judgments that are attached to the property or the current owner\. An owner’s and encumbrance report will also provide property tax information\.

The owner’s and encumbrance report is an “informational report” and is not an opinion, warranty, guarantee, or insurance\. Instead, it is simply a reflection of the public record as it stands on the date of the search\. Unlike a title search report, an owner’s and encumbrance report cannot be used in conjunction with the issuance of a title insurance policy\.

title: Items not included in search unless expressly requested
parent_hierarchy: Items not included in search unless expressly requested
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-30 - Items not included in search unless expressly requested
text: It is important to note that the Company’s title search products do not address corporate status \(found on the Mississippi Secretary of State [website](https://corp.sos.ms.gov/corp/portal/c/page/corpBusinessIdSearch/portal.aspx?&clear=1)\), bankruptcy proceedings \(found on [PACER](https://pacer.login.uscourts.gov/csologin/login.jsf)\), water, garbage and sewer charges \(found in a separate index or printouts\), UCC\-1 filings \(found on the Mississippi Secretary of State [website](http://business.sos.ms.gov/star/portal/msbsd/page/login/portal.aspx)\), personal property taxes or special assessments including, but not limited to, street lighting assessments \(found in the tax collector’s office\) or any other matter not ordinarily found in the official public land records of the county in which the real property is located\. The Company’s title search products also do not include a search of the buyer’s name unless specifically requested at the time the title search product is ordered\.

This title search product is furnished by First American Abstract Company \("First American"\) for the purpose of \(a\) in the case of a full search report or update report relating to the full search report, determining insurability of title to the real property described herein, or \(b\) in the case of a current owner report or informational report, determining the last recorded owner of the real property, the legal description of the real property, and/or any open liens, mortgages, lis pendens and judgments that are attached to the real property\. This title search product is to be relied upon by the addressee only, and cannot be relied upon by any other person or entity or for any other purpose\. This title search product does not insure or warrant the validity or enforceability of any document referenced herein, nor is it intended to be a policy of title insurance, an opinion of title or any other type of guaranty or warranty of title\.

This title search product does not address corporate status, bankruptcy proceedings, water, garbage and sewer charges, personal property taxes or special assessments \(including, but not limited to, street lighting assessments\) or any other matter not ordinarily found in the official public land records of the county in which the real property is located\.

Any title defects, liens, encumbrances or other matters affecting title which are not disclosed by this title search product but are known to or discovered by any person or entity relying on this title search product must be included in any subsequent title insurance commitment, policy or endorsement, or attorney's certificate issued thereby and the party failing to include the information shall indemnify First American, First American Title Insurance Company or any other person or entity sustaining a loss or damage for such omission\.

Liability for any error or omission in this title search product is limited to the addressee only\. In the event a title insurance policy is issued by First American Title Insurance Company in reliance upon this title search product \(full search reports and update reports relating to the full search reports only\), then liability is limited to losses as the same may be determined by the terms of the policy issued by First American Title Insurance Company\. __FIRST AMERICAN'S MAXIMUM CUMULATIVE LIABILITY FOR ANY LOSS OR DAMAGE ARISING OUT OF ANY ERROR OR OMISSION IN THIS TITLE SEARCH PRODUCT, WHETHER IN CONTRACT, TORT OR OTHERWISE, SHALL BE LIMITED TO, IN THE CASE OF A FULL SEARCH REPORT OR UPDATE REPORT RELATING TO THE FULL SEARCH REPORT, THE LESSER OF TWENTY TIMES THE SEARCH FEE OR ONE HUNDRED THOUSAND DOLLARS \($100,000\.00\), OR IN THE CASE OF A CURRENT OWNER REPORT OR INFORMATIONAL REPORT, THE LESSER OF TWO TIMES THE SEARCH FEE OR ONE THOUSAND DOLLARS \($1,000\.00\)\.__

title: Obtaining a prior First American Owner’s Policy
parent_hierarchy: Obtaining a prior First American Owner’s Policy
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-35 - Obtaining a prior First American Owner’s Policy

title: Policies which may not be used as base title
parent_hierarchy: Policies which may not be used as base title
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-36 - Policies which may not be used as base title

title: Search period
text: If a prior Owner’s Policy is being used as base title, Issuing Agents must ensure that the current search date begins no less than 180 days prior to the effective date of the Owner’s Policy\. In other words, if the effective date of the starter policy is July 1, 2017, then the start date for the search will be January 1, 2017\. As such, when a search request is submitted to an abstractor, the Issuing Agent will need to specify the appropriate beginning search start date\. If the vesting deed is not shown in the search, Issuing Agents should require the search be certified back to the time the vesting deed was filed of record\.

title: Policy thresholds
text:
If the amount of the prior Owner’s Policy does not exceed $5,000,000, the Issuing Agent may use the policy as base title, unless the proposed policy exceeds the amount of the prior Owner’s Policy by more than 150%\.

If the amount of the proposed policy exceeds either $5,000,000 or the amount of the prior Owner’s Policy by more than 150%, then the Issuing Agent must seek approval from Underwriting Counsel before issuing a commitment or policy based on a search using a prior Owner’s Policy as base title\.

title: Standard and specific exceptions are required
parent_hierarchy: Standard and specific exceptions are required
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-39 - Standard and specific exceptions are required
text:
Each of the standard exceptions 1\-6 must be inserted into the commitment and excepted in the proposed policy unless all of the applicable requirements to delete the same from the new policy are satisfied\.

Any specific exceptions shown in Schedule B of the prior Owner’s Policy being used as base title must also be inserted into the commitment and excepted in the proposed policy unless the Issuing Agent has evidence that they have been cleared of record\. Copies of each of the specific exceptions listed in the prior policy must be obtained and reviewed\.

Special circumstances including bankruptcy, death, or guardianship of a party in the chain of title will require a name search for a more extensive period\.

title: Issuing Agent’s responsibility to evaluate prior policy
parent_hierarchy: Issuing Agent’s responsibility to evaluate prior policy
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-40 - Issuing Agent’s responsibility to evaluate prior policy
text: The primary responsibility rests with the Issuing Agent for determining whether a particular Owner’s Policy is acceptable under the requirements set forth in this manual\. The reliability of a particular Owner’s Policy is affected by the examining reputation and integrity of the Issuing Agent who issued the prior Owner’s Policy\. The Issuing Agent should carefully exam the prior policy to see who issued it and to see if the policy appears acceptable on its face\. The Issuing Agent should also consider whether there are known title problems underlying the property or in the property’s general area and the type of the previously issued policy\. If the prior Owner’s Policy was issued by an Issuing Agent that is no longer an agent of the Company or has an unfavorable reputation, then the prior Owner’s Policy should not be used as a base title\.

title: Overview
text: This chapter covers easements, profits, and licenses, which are all types of interest in real property that provide a right of entry or use of another’s land\. The purpose of this chapter is to provide a basic understanding of the how easements, profits, and licenses are created, the rights and obligations associated with each type of interest, and when and how these types of interest may be transferred\.

title: Learning Objectives
text:
After completing the assigned readings, you should be able to:

- Explain the differences between easements, licenses, and profits
- Describe different ways to create easements
- Define the rights created by an easement
- Discuss the transferability of easements

title: Key Terms and Concepts
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-68 - Key Terms and Concepts
text:
Below is a list of key terms and concepts introduced in this chapter:

Affirmative easement

Easement by grant

License

Covenant

Easement by implication

Negative easement

Dominant estate / tenement

Easement by necessity

Profit \(profit à prendre\)

Easement

Easement by reservation

Servient estate / tenement

Easement appurtenant

Easement in gross

title: Historical Development
text:
Property law recognizes three types of real servitudes: easements, restrictive covenants, and equitable servitudes\. Each of these types of obligations can pass from the owner of an estate to subsequent purchasers, a concept known as “running with the land\.” The first of these servitudes recognized in common law was the easement, which traces its origins back to Roman law\.

It wasn’t until the early 1800s that English courts began to recognize easements as affirmative rights to enter and use the land of another\. However, no general theory of easements existed at the time\. Before the mid\-1800s, England only recognized affirmative easements and with few exceptions did not allow private restrictions on the use of another’s land\. This limitation reflected the two social policy concerns regarding servitudes that continue to influence current law\. First, notice of restrictions to subsequent purchasers of land\. Second, potential restrictions on alienability\. During this period, lack of notice to purchasers of land posed a real danger with respect to private restrictions on land use because England lacked an effective system of recording titles\. While an affirmative easement for access could be easily observed, negative easements, such as prohibitions on certain types of farming, were not detectable by viewing alone\. Because a servitude bound a subsequent purchaser, regardless of notice, once land was purchased, English courts strictly construed formal requirements for the running of servitudes of any sort\.

Until the mid\-1800s, the United States followed the English philosophy of strictly limiting private restrictions on land and U\.S\. servitude law largely mirrored English law\. Both English and U\.S\. law discouraged the use of servitudes, viewing them as unreasonable restrictions on alienation\. See Proprietors of the Church in Brattle Square v\. Moses Grant, 69 Mass\. \(1 Gray\) 142, 148 \(1855\) \(stating the legal policy in favor of alienable property which “aims to secure the free and unembarrassed disposition of real property”\)\.

Toward the end of the 1800s, however, suburban communities began to form on the outside of large industrial cities and people looked for ways to protect the peaceful environment surrounding their homes\. Landowners had no way to ensure that a new neighbor did not move in and build a factory next door to their home\. As a result both English and U\.S\. courts began developing equitable servitudes and restrictive covenants as methods of private zoning that permitted landowners to restrict the use of the land\. It was around this time that the law developed in English and U\.S\. courts began to diverge\.

While notice and restrictions on alienability continued to be the paramount concerns of English courts regarding servitudes, for U\.S\. courts notice was a diminishing concern\. A public recording system for land ownership and conveyances was established early in the settlement of the United States with the first recording act being adopted by the Massachusetts Bay Colony in 1640\. After the Civil War reliance on the public recording system became the norm\. With a reliable recording system in place, land purchasers were provided notice and prospective land purchasers had the burden of checking the record for a particular estate\. While every state had effective recording systems that addressed concerns over notice, U\.S\. courts still relied on the English doctrines designed to protect purchasers against invisible servitudes\.

As the United States entered the 1900s, concerns regarding servitudes began to shift from notice to the social policy underlying restrictions on the use of land\. Courts throughout the United States began to subscribe to one of two schools of thoughts regarding servitudes\. The first was that allowing private land restrictions that would bind subsequent purchasers restricted alienability and the free use of land was socially undesirable\. The second was that private land restrictions were a type of private zoning that tended to increase the value of land\. As a result, courts began modifying conveyancing rules and treating servitudes as property interests rather than creatures of contract\. The application of doctrines varied greatly from one jurisdiction to the next\.

title: Historical Development
text:
By the early 1900s, the confusion created by the varying restrictions on the different forms of servitudes led to an evolution in property law that made easements, restrictive covenants, and equitable servitudes largely interchangeable\. The former distinctions among the types of servitudes deteriorated as courts applied both equitable and legal principles to each\. Ultimately, the Restatement of the Law of Property adopted a restrictive view of servitudes and advocated giving the courts more discretion to invalidate them\.

The Restatement \(Third\) of Property \(Servitudes\) defines a __servitude __as a legal device that creates a right or an obligation that runs with land or an interest in land\. __Running with land __means that the right or obligation passes automatically to successive owners or occupiers of the land or the interest in land with which the right or obligation runs\. A right that runs with land is called a __benefit __and the interest in land with which it runs may be called the __dominant estate__\. An obligation that runs with land is called a __burden __and the interest in land with which it runs may be called the __servient estate__\.

title: Easements Generally
text:
An __easement __is a nonpossessory right to use another's land for a specific purpose which does not interfere with the owner's use of the property\. McDonald v\. Board of Mississippi Levee Com'rs, 646 F\. Supp\. 449, 468 \(N\.D\. Miss\. 1986\), judgment aff'd, 832 F\.2d 901 \(5th Cir\. 1987\)\. When an easement exists, two

parties are involved\. The holder of the easement and the landowner whose use of the land is subject to the rights of the easement holder\. These two parties simultaneously make use of the same land\.

There are generally two types of easements\. First, an easement appurtenant\. Second, an easement in gross\. Classifying an easement as appurtenant or in gross is important when assessing transferability and succession\.

title: Easement Appurtenant
text:
An __easement appurtenant __is an easement that benefits a particular parcel of land, rather than conferring a personal benefit upon the holder of the easement, and that runs with the land\. For an appurtenant easement to exist, there must be at least two parcels of land\. Browder v\. Graham, 204 Miss\. 773, 38 So\. 2d 188, 189 \(1948\)\. The parcel benefited by the easement is called the dominant estate\. Id\. The parcel burdened with the easement is called the servient estate\. Id\.

The owner of the dominant estate may use an easement on the servient estate\. The land that is benefited by the easement is the __dominant estate __or the __dominant tenement__\. The land that is burdened by the easement is the __servient estate __or __servient tenement__\. An easement appurtenant is usually located next to or near the servient estate\. The easement and the dominant estate must be held by the same party for the easement to be appurtenant\.

title: Easement Appurtenant
text:
The most common example of an appurtenant easement is a driveway across a servient estate connecting the dominant estate to a public road or thruway\. In the above example, assume that the owners of both Lot A and Lot B need access to the street located at the east end of the figure\. The driveway is the subject of the easement that grants access to the owners of Lot A and Lot B to cross Lot C to gain access to the street\. The owner of Lot A has an easement appurtenant to both Lots B and Lot C\. Lot A is the dominant estate, and Lots B and C are the servient estates\. The owner of Lot B would need an easement appurtenant to cross Lot C\. Lot C is the servient estate to both Lot a and Lot B\. Lot B is both a dominant estate and a servient estate to different property owners\.

An appurtenant easement cannot be separated from the land it serves\. Wisconsin Ave\. Properties, Inc\. v\. First Church of Nazarene of Vicksburg, 768 So\.2d 914, 918 \(Miss\. 2000\)\. An appurtenant easement can only be conveyed by the conveyance of the dominant estate\. Id\. However, an appurtenant easement requires no written conveyance because it is a vested right for successive holders of the dominant tenement and remains binding on successive holders of the servient tenement\. Pitts v\. Foster, 743 So\.2d 1066, 1069 \(¶ 8\) \(Miss\.Ct\.App\.1999\)\. By acquiring a dominant estate, one has already paid for and procured the legal right of access to and from that parcel\. Broadhead v\. Terpening, 611 So\.2d 949, 955 \(Miss\.1992\)\. In other words, an appurtenant easement “runs with the land\.” Id\. at 954\. Therefore, a conveyance document

transferring ownership to the dominant and servient estates, such as a deed, generally does not need to reference the recorded easement for it to transfer\.

It should be noted that easement rights appurtenant to the insured property creating rights in or over adjoining premises, are not generally insured under the policy by definition of the word “Land” in the Conditions portion of the policy, which limits coverage under the policy to the property described by the legal description referred to in the commitment/policy\. In those instances, where the existence of an easement is essential to the use and enjoyment of the insured premises \(i\.e\., an easement for access\), the examiner must examine title to the property over which the easement passes, identify the record owner, as well as any liens, encumbrances or defects affecting said easement, and certify that title to the easement is vested in the insured owner\. In order that an easement be insured, said easement must exist by grant or by reservation in an instrument duly recorded; it must be said to “run with the land” or “be appurtenant thereto;” and it should be conveyed “together with” the premises to be insured\.

title: Easement in Gross
text:
An __easement in gross __is an easement that benefits a person, regardless of whether that person owns any land at all\. An easement in gross benefits an individual or entity personally, rather than benefitting a dominant estate\. Typically, easements in gross are not between adjacent property owners\.

An easement in gross is sometimes described as a personal right or interest because there is a servient estate, but no dominant estate\. This means that an easement in gross terminates upon death of the individual owner or the cessation of a business\. However, an easement in gross may be transferable where the easement is in writing and explicitly assignable\.

\[Need example graphic of EIG\]

The most common examples of easements in gross are utility easements\. In the above example,

obtains an easement to install utility lines through the homeowner’s front yard\. The utility has an

easement in gross\.

Transfer is not automatic and in most cases limited to the original holder\.

Title to an easement in gross that is non\-commercial in nature is generally not insurable and is considered an exception to the title of any property it burdens\.

title: Rights and Duties Created by Easements
parent_hierarchy: Rights and Duties Created by Easements
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-74 - Rights and Duties Created by Easements
text:
Every easement contains a right to do such things as are reasonably necessary to fully enjoy the easement\. The extent to which these rights may be exercised depends on the language in the grant and if such rights were limited by the servient owner\. The easement holder's use should not seriously burden the servient owner, except for the specific easement purpose\.

The use in an express grant is determined by the terms of the grant in light of the surrounding circumstances\. When an easement is granted for a specific purpose, the grantee is restricted to that purpose, even when other purposes are not restricted\. The limits of the use in an express grant may not be enlarged beyond that grant\. Common examples include access over a defined area or the right to place utilities in a defined area\.

When an express grant is made in general terms, uses of the easement must be reasonably necessary and convenient, but may burden the servient estate as little as possible\. A reasonable use can be defined as a use that does not unreasonably prejudice the rights of others\. Courts look to the local situation, public usage, and nature and condition of the servient estate in determining proper use\. Where an express grant is made in general terms but both parties consent to a use, that use is fixed and is limited to

the particular manner in which it is being enjoyed\. Common examples include access over an entire tract or from one point to another or a blanket utility easement\.

The servient owner has the right of full dominion over the use of the land for the purpose of the easement purpose\. The servient owner may use the land in a way that may interfere with the easement as long as the servient owner’s use is not destructive of, or so burdensome as to destroy the rights of the easement owner\. The servient owner is only required to abstain from interfering with easement or from hindering or obstructing the easement owner’s use of the easement\.

The easement owner has a duty to use ordinary care in order to avoid injury to the servient estate\. However, it is difficult for the servient owner to recover damages resulting from use of an easement\. The servient owner must show that the easement owner acted with willfulness or negligence in the use of the easement\.

title: Distinguishing between Appurtenant or In Gross
parent_hierarchy: Distinguishing between Appurtenant or In Gross
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-75 - Distinguishing between Appurtenant or In Gross
text: Sometimes it is difficult to identify whether a particular easement is appurtenant \(runs with the land it benefits\) or in gross \(exists independently\)\. Whether a particular easement is classified as an appurtenant easement or easement in gross depends mainly on its nature and the intention of the parties creating it\. If the easement by its nature is an appropriate and useful adjunct to the land conveyed, and there is nothing to show that the parties intended it to be a more personal right, then it should be an easement appurtenant and not an easement in gross\. Easements in gross are not favored in the law, and an easement will never be presumed as personal when it may fairly be construed as appurtenant, rather than in gross\.

title: Creation of Easements
text: In Mississippi, there are three common law methods of creating easements: by grant, by prescription, or by implication/necessity\. Simcox v\. Hunt, 874 So\.2d 1010, 1017\(¶ 32\) \(Miss\. Ct\. App\. 2004\)\. In addition, a fourth method of creating an easement exist in Miss\. Code Ann\. § 65\-7\-201\.

title: Express Easement
text:
The most common and perhaps best method of creating an easement is by express grant or reservation\. Because easements are interests in real property, they come within the purview of the statute of frauds\. Thus, at a minimum, to successfully create an easement by express grant or reservation, the instrument creating the easement must be in writing and signed by the creator of the easement\. In addition, the instrument must identify the servient estate and reflect the grantor’s intent to create an easement\.

A grantor may reserve an easement for himself in an instrument used to convey the fee\. However, under common law, when a single instrument is used to reserve an easement in favor of a third party and, simultaneously, to convey the burdened estate to another, then the intended easement is invalid\. 4 Powell on Real Property § 34\.04 \(2019\)\. This is because historically neither a “reservation” nor an “exception” could be used to create an easement in favor of a third person\. Id\. To effectuate the transfer of an easement to a third\-party and avoid the common\-law prohibition, two conveyances would be required\. One to convey the easement to the intended beneficiary and another to subsequently transfer the servient estate to the intended transferee\. Mississippi treats a reservation in favor of a third party as an exception retained by the grantor, rather than allowing the grantee to take the parcel free and clear of the easement\. Cook v\. Farley, 15 So\. 2d 352, 355\-56 \(Miss\. 1943\)\. In other words, the conveyed property remains burdened by the easement for the benefit of the grantor’s land\.

A property owner can create an express easement by grant or reservation\. A “grant” of an easement occurs when a property owner gives an easement to a dominant estate\. For example, if a common owner of two parcels sells the parcel away from the public road and retains the front parcel that has access, such owner would grant an easement for access to the buyer of the rear parcel\. Conversely, if the same owner

was selling the front parcel and keeping the rear parcel, that owner would want to “reserve” an easement

for himself or herself for access over the front parcel\.

A grant or reservation can be by separate instrument or within a deed\. Even if a sale of property occurs concurrently with granting of the easement, it is preferable to have the easement set forth by separate instrument rather than in the deed\. There are three reasons to support this method\. First, any discussion regarding the scope of use or other details does not fit neatly into the deed, and a practitioner is constrained in his or her ability to set forth the detail that may be necessary\. Second, though acceptance of an easement by the dominant estate would imply acceptance of the terms in most cases, it is preferable to see both parties’ signatures actually on the document, and a deed is a one\-party document\. A separate document is particularly important when the dominant estate owner is making express promises such as maintenance requirements\. Third, the easement is much less likely to be missed by a title examiner when it is a separate document clearly providing the names of both the grantor, grantee, and descriptions of the dominant estate, the servient estate, and the easement itself\.

The existence or nonexistence, nature, and extent of an express easement are “determined by the language of the deed \[or other instrument\], taken in connection with the circumstances existing at the time of making it\.” Favre v\. Jourdan River Estates, 148 So\.3d 361, 368 \(¶ 20\) \(Miss\. 2014\) \(citing Lanier v\. Booth, 50 Miss\. 410, 414 \(1874\)\)\.

Descriptions of easements may be fairly general, they may include a metes\-and\-bounds description, the use of distances and directions, or references to natural or artificial monuments; however, “\[a\]ny description of an easement needs accuracy and clarity\.” Warren v\. Derivaux, 996 So\.2d 729, 736 \(¶ 15\) \(Miss\. 2008\) \(quoting Moran v\. Sims, 873 So\.2d 1067, 1070 \(¶ 15\) \(Miss\.Ct\.App\.2004\)\)\.

title: Express Easement
text: Where an instrument grants an easement over land owned by multiple co\-owners, all of the co\-owners must act in concert to burden their property with the easement/servitude\. Since a grantor cannot establish an easement in an estate that the grantor does not own, the holder of an undivided interest, such as a tenant in common or a joint tenant, cannot create an easement that binds the shares of the other co\-owners\. 3 Tiffany, Law of Real Property \(3d ed\.\) § 776; *See also *Texas Mortg\. Co\. v\. Phillips Petroleum Co\., 470 F\.2d 497, 499 \(5th Cir\. 1972\)\. If fewer than all of the owners of an estate attempt to create a servitude burdening that estate, the attempt does not create an easement, but does create rights enforceable against the owners who joined in the attempt\. Restatement \(Third\) of Property \(Servitudes\) § 2\.3 \(2000\)\. The attempt may provide the basis for later creation of a servitude, either by estoppel of the other owners, or on partition of the estate\. Id\.

title: Easement by Prescription
text:
Obtaining an easement by prescription is closely analogous to acquiring title to land by adverse possession\. The fundamental difference between the two is that a prescriptive easement is for the use of, not the ownership of, the land\.

The standard and burden of proof to establish a prescriptive easement is the same as a claim of adverse possession of land\. Mayton v\. Oliver, 247 So\.3d 312, 322 \(¶ 32\) \(Miss\. Ct\. App\. 2017\)\. To acquire property by prescriptive easement the claimant must show that the possession was: \(1\) open, notorious, and visible; \(2\) hostile; \(3\) under claim of ownership; \(4\) exclusive; \(5\) peaceful; and \(6\) continuous and uninterrupted for ten years\. Biddix v\. McConnell, 911 So\.2d 468, 475 \(¶ 18\) \(Miss\. 2005\)\. All six elements must be proven for a prescriptive easement to be valid\. Sharp v\. White, 749 So\.2d 41, 43 \(¶ 9\) \(Miss\. 1999\)\. These elements must be proven by clear and convincing evidence\. Mayton, 247 So\.3d at 322 \(¶ 32\)\. Clear and convincing evidence is such a high standard of proof that even the overwhelming weight of the evidence does not rise to the same level\. Id\.

In order to establish an easement by prescription, it is not necessary that the way has been in constant use, day and night, but it may be established by such use as business or pleasure may require\.” Threlkeld v\. Sisk, 992 So\.2d 1232, 1238 \(¶ 17\) \(Miss\. Ct\. App\. 2008\) \(quoting Browder v\. Graham, 204 Miss\.

773, 780, 38 So\.2d 188 \(1948\)\)\.

“Hostile” use is use that is inconsistent with the title of the servient\-estate owner\. Threlkeld, 992 So\.2d at 1239 \(¶ 18\)\. Use of property that is permissive prevents a prescriptive easement from forming\. Id\. Use by express or implied permission or license, no matter how long continued, cannot ripen into an easement by prescription, since adverse use, as distinguished from permissive use, is lacking\. Id\.

One claiming a prescriptive easement need not claim to own the land itself, but he or she must claim to own an easement\. Threlkeld, 992 So\.2d at 1239 \(¶ 21\) \(quoting Delancey v\. Mallette, 912 So\.2d 483, 488

\(¶ 16\) \(Miss\. Ct\. App\. 2005\)\)\.

“Exclusive” does not mean that no one else used the road, but that ‘the use was consistent with an exclusive claim to the right to use\.’ Threlkeld, 992 So\.2d at 1239\-40 \(¶ 22\) \(quoting Moran v\. Sims, 873 So\.2d 1067, 1069 \(¶ 10\) \(Miss\. Ct\. App\. 2004\)\)\. The distinction to be made when using the term exclusive as it relates to a prescriptive easement does not mean to keep all others out, but to show a right to use the land above other members of the general public\. Keener Properties L\.L\.C\. v\. Wilson, 912 So\.2d 954, 957 \(¶ 8\) \(Miss\. 2005\)\.

“Peaceful” is defined as marked by, conducive to, or enjoying peace, quiet, or calm\. Biddix v\. McConnell, 911 So\.2d 468, 477 \(¶ 25\) \(Miss\. 2005\) \(quoting Webster's Third International Dictionary 1160

title: Easement by Prescription
text:
\(1986\)\)\.

A prescriptive easement vests when the adverse use has been continuous and uninterrupted for a period of ten years\. Threlkeld, 992 So\.2d at 1240 \(¶ 24\) \(quoting Delancey, 912 So\.2d at 489 \(¶ 18\)\)\.

The requirements for an easement by prescription are similar to those for obtaining title by adverse possession\. However, the claimant only obtains a right to use the land, not fee title\.

Such easements are not favored by law, and the burden is on the claimant to prove his/her case by clear and convincing evidence\. The scope of the easement is based primarily on the use that gave rise to the easement\. A claim to such an easement can be refuted if the owner can show the use was by permission\. In such cases, an exception should be made to this possibility:

__Plat of survey by \[●\] \[name of surveyor\], \[R\.L\.S\.\]\[P\.L\.S\.\], dated \[●\], shows \[●\] \[identify\]__

__located on the Land\.__

An easement existing or supposed to exist by prescription or by operation of law is generally not insurable as appurtenant to the property and most underwriters require an appropriate exception be made when the property being insured is the servient tenement\.

While the requirements are basically the same for adverse possession and prescriptive easements, adverse possession is a right to the title of the land whereas, prescriptive easements are a right to an easement\.

title: Easement by Necessity \(Implication\)
text:
There are two types of implication easements: easements essential to the enjoyment of the land and easements by necessity\. Fike v\. Shelton, 860 So\.2d 1227, 1230 \(Miss\. Ct\. App\. 2003\)\. “An easement by necessity arises by operation of law when part of a commonly\-owned tract of land is severed in a way that

renders either portion of the property inaccessible except by passing over the other portion or by trespassing on the lands of another\.” Id\. \(citing Broadhead v\. Terpening, 611 So\.2d 949, 954 \(Miss\.1992\)\)\.

title: Easement by Necessity \(Implication\)
text:
The most common example of an easement by necessity is a driveway across the land of a grantor who conveys a landlocked parcel\. In the above example, A owns a rectangular parcel bordered on the north, east, and west by privately owned land and on the south by a public street\. A conveys to B a strip of her land on the northern boundary\. If A fails to grant an express easement, B will acquire an easement by necessity across the southern portion of the parcel retained by A\.

A claimant seeking an easement by necessity has the burden of proof and must establish that he is entitled to a right of way across another's land\. Davidson v\. Collins, 195 So\.3d 825, 827 \(Miss\. Ct\. App\. 2015\)\. An easement by necessity requires proof that \(1\) the easement is necessary; \(2\) the dominant and servient estates were once part of a commonly owned parcel; \(3\) the implicit right\-of\-way arose at the time of severance from the common owner\. Borne v\. Estate of Carraway, 118 So\.3d 571, 584 \(Miss\. 2013\)\. To satisfy this burden, the claimants must show strict necessity; that they possess no other means of access to their property\. Haik v\. Gammill, 122 So\.3d 771, 778 \(Miss\. Ct\. App\. 2013\)\.

An easement by necessity may be created by proving only reasonable necessity rather than absolute physical necessity\. Evanna Plantation, Inc\. v\. Thomas, 999 So\.2d 442, 446 \(Miss\. App\. 2009\)\. In determining what is reasonably necessary, the operative consideration is whether an alternative would involve disproportionate expense and inconvenience\. Id\. An alternative would involve disproportionate expense and inconvenience if the expense of making the means of access available would exceed the entire value of the property to which access was sought\. Id\.

An easement by necessity has a right of access that is appurtenant to the dominant parcel and travels with the land, so long as the necessity exists\. Fike v\. Shelton, 860 So\.2d 1227, 1230–31 \(Miss\. App\. 2003\)\. Unlike a statutory right of way – which requires compensation – by acquiring the dominant estate, one has already paid for and procured the legal right of access to and from that parcel\. Id\. The easement or right\-of\-way will last as long as the necessity exists and will terminate after other access to the landlocked parcel becomes available\. Id\.

Easements by necessity and by implication are appurtenant to the dominant estate and run with land\. Broadhead v\. Terpening, 611 So\.2d 949, 954 \(Miss\. 1992\)\.

In addition to showing severance of title and necessity, a party must also demonstrate that it has unsuccessfully attempted to secure a private easement across all other surrounding property by contract or deed\. Ward v\. Trimac Investments, LLC, 78 So\. 3d 341, 344 \(Miss\. Ct\. App\. 2011\)

title: Statutory Rights of Way
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-80 - Statutory Rights of Way
text: As an alternative to the easement by necessity, Mississippi has enacted legislation with the goal of providing relief for owners of landlocked parcels of property\. Miss\. Code Ann\. § 65\-7\-201 reads as follows:

title: When any person shall desire to have a private road laid out through the land of another, when necessary for ingress and egress, he shall apply by petition, stating the facts and reasons, to the special court of eminent domain created under Section 11\-27\-3 of the county where the land or part of it is located, and the case shall proceed as nearly as possible as provided in Title 11, Chapter 27 for the condemnation of private property for public use\. The court sitting without a jury shall determine the reasonableness of the application\. The owner of the property shall be a necessary party to the proceedings\. If the court finds in favor of the petitioner, all damages that the jury determines the landowner should be compensated for shall be assessed against and shall be paid by the person applying for the private road, and he shall pay all the costs and expenses incurred in the proceedings\.

text:
This statute allows the condemnation of a private right of way over neighboring lands and can be useful to those property owners who are landlocked but fail to establish the requisite elements of a common\-law easement by necessity\. For example, if a property owner cannot prove that the landlocked condition resulted from a severance of a tract that had been in prior common ownership, as required for an easement by necessity, then the owner of the landlocked parcel can use Miss\. Code Ann\. § 65\-7\-201 to obtain the easement\. However, there are limitations to obtaining a statutory right of way\.

First, in order to obtain a statutory right of way, the petitioner carries the burden of proving the proposed private road is necessary\. Hooks v\. George County, 748 So\. 2d 678, 683 \(Miss\.1999\)\. The showing required is only that the right of way is “reasonably necessary,” as opposed to absolutely necessary\. Quinn v\. Holly, 146 So\. 2d 357, 359 \(1962\)\. However, although absolute necessity need not be shown, “real necessity” is still required, and a private road may not be granted for convenience or to save expense\. Ganier v\. Mansour, 766 So\.2d 3, 7 \(¶ 14\) \(Miss\. Ct\. App\. 2000\)\. Because ‘the right to control and use of one's property is a sacred right not to be lightly invaded or disturbed,’ in order to invade this right and be granted a private road over \[another’s\] property, a \[petitioner must\] show ‘real necessity, not just mere convenience\.’ ” Davidson v\. Collins, 195 So\.3d 825, 826\-27 \(Miss\. App\. 2015\) \(finding that there was not a sufficient showing of reasonable necessity for an easement when the petitioner only utilized the property in the summer months for purely recreational purposes, and there was a public boat lunch within two hundred yards of the sandbar and dock area\)\.

Second, to show necessity, the petitioner must show that the property has no access to a public road and that the petitioner has attempted to secure a right of way by contract or grant\. Ward v\. Trimac Investments, LLC, 78 So\.3d 341, 344 \(Miss\. App\. 2011\)\. Specifically, “the landlocked landowner must allege and show that he has been unable to obtain a reasonable right\-of\-way from all of the surrounding property owners\.” Rotenberry v\. Renfro, 214 So\.2d 275, 278 \(Miss\.1968\); Whitefort v\. Homochitto Lumber Co\., 130 Miss\. 14, 26, 93 So\. 437, 439 \(1922\)\.

Third, under this statutory scheme for acquiring access, the petitioner must compensate the landowner over whose land he is given a right of way by paying the landowner the fair value of any land taken and any damage that might accrue to the remainder of the landowner's property\. Alpaugh v\. Moore, 568 So\.2d 291, 295 \(Miss\.1990\); Quinn v\. Holly, 146 So\.2d 357, 358 \(1962\)\. In addition, the petitioner must pay for all the costs and expenses incurred in proceedings before the board of supervisors\. Broadhead v\. Terpening, 611 So\.2d 949, 955 \(Miss\.1992\)\. Miss\. Code Ann\. § 65\-7\-201 does not apply to a common law easement by necessity because it requires the petitioner to compensate the landowner for the taking of his land\. Fike v\. Shelton, 860 So\.2d 1227, 1232 \(Miss\. App\. 2003\)

Code Ann\. § 65\-7\-201 to petition the special court of eminent domain to establish a private road does not extend to condemning property within an incorporated municipality\. High v\. Kuhn, 240 So\.3d 1198, 1199 \(Miss\. 2017\)\. Section 110 of the Mississippi Constitution prohibits condemning for a statutory private road any property located within an incorporated town or city\. See Miss\. Const\. art\. 4, § 110\.

title: Easement by Reference to Plats and Maps
parent_hierarchy: Easement by Reference to Plats and Maps
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-82 - Easement by Reference to Plats and Maps
text:
Like most other states, Mississippi also recognizes an easement created by reference to a plat or map\. See McBroom v\. Jackson County, 154 So\.3d 827, 834 \(Miss\. 2014\)\. This easement arises when a developer conveys lots in a subdivision and the deed references a plat or map indicating common open areas within the subdivision\. Each purchaser obtains an easement in these open and public areas delineated in the plat or map, such as streets and alleys\. These easements are based on the principle of estoppel because prospective purchasers are induced to purchase lots in reliance on the grantor’s representations regarding the open public areas referenced in the plat\. *Conveyance of Lot with Reference to Map or Plat as Giving Purchaser Rights in Indicated Streets, Alleys, or Areas Not Abutting His Lot*, 7 A\.L\.R\.2d 607, 613\-16, 650\-65\.

There are three divergent views regarding the extent of the scope of an easement created by reference to a plat or map\. The first approach, which is referred to as the “broad view,” is that the private right of way extends to all streets, alleys, parks, or other open areas delineated in the plat\. A second view holds that the extent of the private right of way is limited to those streets and alleys that the lot owner could reasonably believe would materially benefit the lot owner\. In other words, the deprivation of the use of the road, alley, or common area would decrease the value of the lot\. This view is commonly referred to as the “intermediate view” or the “beneficial rule\.” A third even more restrictive approach holds that such private right of way is limited to the abutting streets and those areas necessary to give the grantee access to a public highway\. This view is commonly referred to as the “necessary view\.” Mississippi appears to have adopted the broad view – a grantee to whom a conveyance was made by reference to a map or plat acquires a private right of way over all streets and alleys shown on such plat\. See Skates v\. Bryant, 863 So\.2d 907, 910 \(Miss\. 2003\); Skrmetta v\. Moore, 202 Miss\. 585, 30 So\. 2d 53 \(1947\)\.

For a discussion of dedications related to subdivision plats, see [Chapter 20:](#_bookmark204) [Lot and Block Survey](#_bookmark204) [System](#_bookmark204)\.

title: Private or Public Use
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-84 - Private or Public Use
text: Easements may be classified as “private” or “public,” depending on whether they are in favor of an individual or the public at large\. A __private easement __is an easement to an individual or entity, such as an easement between neighbors\. A __public easement __is an easement to a large group of individuals or to the public in general, such as an easement for a public street, an easement for a public park, or the right to navigate a body of water located on private land\. Generally, private easements are appurtenant easements, while public easements are easements in gross\.
