text: In the above example, the driveway across Lot B and Lot C would be a private easement, while the street itself would be a public easement\.

title: Exclusive or Non\-exclusive
text:
Generally, easements are non\-exclusive unless the instrument creating the easement specifically states otherwise\. The servient landowner typically may allow others to use the land, subject to the easement, as long as the use does not interfere with the easement holder’s rights\. For example, a servient land owner may lease its property to a third party\. In this case, the tenant’s rights under the lease are subject to:

- The prior easement agreement\.
- The rights granted to the easement holder in the easement agreement\.

If the servient landowner did not grant an exclusive easement initially, it may grant multiple, unrelated parties the right to use the same easement area provided there is no interference between any of the easement holders\.

title: Exclusive or Non\-exclusive
text: In the above example, the easement across Lot C would need to be non\-exclusive, since the owners of both Lot A and Lot B would use that portion of the driveway to access their respective properties\. However, the easement across Lot B could be, depending on the language in the easement, exclusive in favor of the owner of Lot A\. The street would be non\-exclusive in favor of the public at large\.

title: Duration \(Perpetual or Temporary\)
text:
Unless expressly limited, easements are generally perpetual grants and continue until terminated\. Whether an easement is perpetual or temporary often depends on the type and use of the easement\. For example, utility easements are usually perpetual and continue unless expressly terminated, but other types of easements are limited and often exist for only a limited duration\. Temporary easements include specific language that the easement terminates when the use is no longer necessary\.

The most common example of a __temporary easement __is an easement for construction purposes, since they are needed only during the construction project for which they are created\.

An easement for a particular purpose, while not expressly limited as to time, may prove to be temporary if the stated purpose disappears\. Thus, easements with a stated purpose may not be perpetual\.

title: Affirmative or Negative
text:
Easements typically contain either affirmative or negative covenants that control the servient estate

holder’s rights relating to the burdened property\.

An easement is classified as an __affirmative easement __if the dominant estate holder has the right to use the servient estate for a particular purpose, and the servient estate holder is required to do something \(such as allow the dominant estate holder access over its property\)\. Most easements are affirmative easements because they give the dominant estate holder rights over the servient estate\.

title: Affirmative or Negative
text:
A common example of an affirmative easement is a driveway easement\. In the example above, the owner of Lot A has an affirmative easement over Lot B, since it allows the owner of Lot A to access its property over a designated portion of Lot B\.

A __negative easement __is also sometimes called a restrictive easement\. This type of easement includes a covenant from the servient \(burdened\) landowner not to do something relating to its property, therefore divesting itself of the full use and enjoyment of the land\. The dominant \(benefited\) landowner enjoys the benefit of the restriction\.

title: Affirmative or Negative
text:
The most common examples of negative or restrictive easements are easements for light, air, and view\. A __view easement __restricts the burdened party from building on its land in a way that would block the view to the benefitted party’s parcel\. In the example above, the owner of Lot 1 has a view \(negative\) easement over Lot 2, since it prevents the owner of Lot 2 from building improvements that block the view from Lot 1\. Another type of negative easement is one that gives the dominant landowner the right to require the servient landowner to maintain a fence or other type of property divider \(such as a tree line\) on its property\.

Negative easements are not generally drafted as stand\-alone agreements\. Instead, this type of easement is often included in either a conveyance document, or a declaration of covenants, conditions & restrictions agreement governing a large residential housing development or a planned commercial development\.

title: Location of Easements
text:
In an express easement, the location of the easement is usually specified in the grant\. The legal description is used to plot the easement on a survey\. If the grant does not specifically state the location, the servient owner may select the location of the easement as long as it is reasonable in regard to the dominant owner’s rights\. If the servient owner fails to designate a location for the easement, the dominant owner may choose the location\. In any case, if a specific area has been historically used, the area used would define the location of the easement\. If neither the servient nor the dominant estate designates the location of an easement, as in a “blanket” easement, a judge can decide\. Courts will focus on the intent of the parties when deciding location\. But in all cases, the easement must be reasonable to both parties\. An easement may be relocated by action of the parties, such a mistaken construction of the easement with consent, resulting in a easement by estoppel when the improvements are actually located\.

When there is an implied or prescriptive easement, the location and dimensions are fixed by the actual use of the servient estate\.

title: Transfer of Easements
text:
The primary distinction in determining the transferability of easements depends on whether the easement is appurtenant or in gross\.

Appurtenant easements transfer with the dominant estate unless the original easement agreement or other document of creation states otherwise\. Because an appurtenant easement runs with the land, it transfers with the dominant estate even if the easement is not specifically mentioned in the transferring instrument\. However, counsel should reference the easement in the transfer document\.

Whether an easement in gross is transferable by the easement holder depends on whether the easement is commercial or non\-commercial\. Commercial easements in gross are generally transferable\. Non\-commercial easements in gross are generally not transferable, as they are a right of personal enjoyment for the holder\. When determining the transferability of an easement in gross that is a non\-commercial easement, courts consider both the parties’ intentions and the laws governing such interests\.

title: Expiration/Agreement
text:
Generally, once created, an easement exists in perpetuity unless some specific action is taken to terminate it\. An easement may be terminated when the term stated in the written easement has expired\. This only applies when the easement was created for a limited purpose or period of time, which has elapsed, or modified to include such an expiration provision\. Alternatively, an easement may be terminated if the owner of the dominant estate releases his/her interest in the easement\. Such a release should be in writing

and recorded\. In addition, it is recommended that any agreements to create, modify, amend of terminate an easement be memorialized in a writing sufficient to satisfy the statute of frauds\.

For implied easements, the easement will end when the purpose for which the easement was created has ceased\. For example, an implied easement for access will end when a public road is created on the other side of the property which would provide alternative access\. A septic drainfield easement will end when the property hooks up to the public sewer system\. Distinguish an agreement that terminates at the will of the grantor, which generally is considered to be a license, not an easement\.

title: Abandonment
text: Easements may be terminated by abandonment\. Whether an easement has been abandoned depends on the scope of the original easement\. Lack of use by itself is not abandonment\. In addition, there must be an intent on the grantor’s part to relinquish the easement, and a manifestation of that intent by some affirmative conduct\. Thus, abandonment occurs when use of the easement ends coupled with the clear intent to never use the easement again\. Intent may be inferred by the circumstances\.

title: Merger
text: When one party acquires present possessory fee simple title to both the servient and the dominant tenements, the easement merges into the fee of the servient tenement and is terminated\. Cox v\. Trustmark Nat\. Bank, 733 So\. 2d 353, 355 \(Miss\. Ct\. App\. 1999\)\. Therefore, special care needs to be taken by Issuing Agents to verify that existing easements which may have merged if the property comes under common ownership after the establishment of same, have been properly re\-established if the tract is later divided\.

title: Termination of Necessity
text: An easement by necessity is one which has been implied by the circumstances\. Thus, when there is no longer a necessity, the easement is terminated\.

title: Termination by Prescription
text: An easement by prescription may be terminated by reverse prescription, such as the servient owner’s adverse use of the easement area for the period of prescription\. Although such circumstances may seem unusual, it must be remembered that most easements run in perpetuity, so that successive 10 year prescriptive periods over the course of a century are clearly possible\.

title: Termination by Estoppel
text: If the owner of the servient estate acts to his or her detriment in reasonable reliance on actions of the grantee that indicate the grantee plans to make no further use of the property, then that party may seek a declaration that the easement is terminated\. In support of that request, an allegation of the facts supporting both the reasonableness of the reliance and the resulting detriment would be made that would argue the grantee is estopped by their actions from claiming that the easement should continue\.

title: Termination because of Misuse
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-97 - Termination because of Misuse
text: The owner of the servient estate may obtain an injunction restricting the use of the easement by the holder of the easement if the holder misuses or overburdens the easement area\. Depending on the situation, a court may restrict usage or terminate the easement altogether\.

title: Sale of Servient Estate to Bona Fide Purchaser for Value, without Notice\.
parent_hierarchy: Sale of Servient Estate to Bona Fide Purchaser for Value, without Notice\.
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-98 - Sale of Servient Estate to Bona Fide Purchaser for Value, without Notice\.
text: An easement may also be terminated when the servient owner conveys the servient estate to a purchaser who has neither actual nor constructive notice of the easement’s existence prior to the sale\. Actual notice may be found be either \(1\) written or oral statements or \(2\) by physical evidence existing on the property at the time of conveyance\. Constructive notice may be found when the easement has been recorded in the county land records\.

title: Tax Sale
text:
An easement is different from other encumbrances with regard to tax sales\. Miss\. Code Ann\. § 27\-45\-23; See also Howie v\. Panola\-Quitman Drainage Dist\., 151 So\. 154, 156 \(Miss\. 1933\) \(noting that sale of land for taxes conveys perfect title to purchaser held to convey title in fee simple except in so far as title is qualified by other provisions creating lien\); City of Jackson v\. Ashley, 189 Miss\. 818, 199 So\. 91 \(1940\) \(finding that the restrictive covenants were cut off at the tax sale\)\. Unlike other encumbrances, a tax sale does not extinguish an easement appurtenant, as long as the easement is properly assessed and included in the value of the property prior to the tax sale\. Hearn v\. Autumn Woods Office Park Property Owners Ass’n, 757 So\.2d 155, 162 \(Miss\. 1999\) \(upholding an ingress and egress and parking easement reasoning that the value of the easement was properly accessed to the beneficial estate and deducted from the servient estate which was the subject of the case\)\. When there is no evidence to the contrary, an assessment for tax purposes may be presumed, as a matter of law, to include the value of an easement\. Id\. Only when a dispute arises over whether the value of the easement was included in the assessment of a property acquired by tax deed, will the method for assessing the value of the property become determinative on whether the easement survives a tax sale\. Id\.

In Mississippi, real property must be assessed according to its “true value”\. Miss\. Code Ann\. § 27\-35\-49\. True value refers to the market value, cash value, actual cash value, proper value and value for the purposes of appraisal for ad valorem taxation\. Miss\. Code Ann\. § 27\-35\-50\. At the time of valuation, residential single family property and all other real property must be appraised according to “current use\.” Miss\. Code Ann\. § 27\-35\-50\(4\)\. Thus, where, for example, a servient parcel is subject to an easement for use as a parking lot, a purchaser at a tax sale must overcome the presumption, as a matter of law, that the assessor assessed the value of the land *with the easement *for parking in order to extinguish the easement\.

title: Foreclosure
text: Whether the foreclosure of a mortgage, deed of trust or other security interest has an effect on an easement depends on when the easement was granted\. Where a parcel of land is subject to an easement and is later mortgaged, the easement simply constitutes an exception to title and should be shown as such\. Subsequent foreclosure of the mortgage will not extinguish the easement\. Where, however, an easement is granted over property that is subject to a prior mortgage, deed of trust or other security interest, a foreclosure of the prior mortgage, deed of trust or other security interest will terminate the easement\. Therefore, a subordination agreement should be obtained from the secured party in order to ensure that any subsequent foreclosure of that security interest does not extinguish the junior easement\.

title: Eminent Domain
text: By using its power of eminent domain, the government may take an easement on private property or a servient estate and terminate the easement\. Condemnation of the servient estate can also terminate an easement if the condemnation conflicts with the existence of the easement\. The servient estate owner or the easement holder is entitled to just compensation as a result of the government taking of the property through eminent domain\.

title: License
text:
A __license __is permission to enter the licensor’s property\. Unlike easements, which are subject to the statute of frauds, licenses are created informally\. They are usually temporary and are freely revocable unless the parties otherwise agree\. Licenses do not have possession but only a limited right to use the owner’s land for a particular purpose or activity\. A license is a personal, revocable, and unassignable \(nontransferable\) right\. It is not a interest in land and does not pass with the title to the property\. Licenses may be either oral or written\.

The most common example of a license is a parking garage ticket when entering a parking structure\.

You have been granted a license to park your vehicle\.

Easements should not be confused with licenses\. In deciding whether an easement or license has

been created, the most critical factor is the parties’ intent\. The following elements show intent of a party:

- *Manner of creation of right *\(oral or written\)\. A written agreement is more likely to be an easement, particularly if detailed\. However, the label that parties give the right does not dictate its legal effect\.
- *Nature of right created*\. The creation of a right on a particular portion of the servient estate indicates that an easement was intended\. A more general use right is more likely a license\. A personal right is more likely a license\.
- *Duration of a righ*t\. An express duration indicates an easement\. A shorter term indicated a license\.
- *Amount of consideration, if any, given for right*\. The more consideration paid, the more likely an easement is intended\.
- *Reservation of power to revoke right*\. If there is an express reservation of power to revoke or terminate the grant was likely a license\. A right that continues without any right for the servient estate to terminate is a strong indication of an easement\.
- *Assignability*\. A license is, generally, not assignable\.

title: Profit à prendre
text:
A __profit à prendre __is the right to enter and remove timber, minerals, or other substances from land in the possession of another\. It is not technically an easement, however, it has the same effect as an easement because it grants the holder the right to use and go on the land of another\. To be valid and enforceable, it must satisfy the same requirements of an easement\. A profit à prendre grants the beneficiary:

- A license to go on to the land of another\.
- Authorization to take certain things away from or off of the land\.

Examples of a profit à prendre include the right to:

- Farm on the land of another and take crops from the land\.
- Mine or take minerals from the land of another\.
- Graze or herd livestock over the land of another\.
- Hunt or fish on the land of another and take wildlife from the land\.

title: Overview
text: This chapter covers the Public Land Survey System \(“PLSS”\), also known as the U\.S\. Rectangular Land Survey, the Congressional Survey, the Federal Rectangular Survey, the Rectangular Survey, and the Government Survey\. The purpose of this chapter is to provide a basic understanding of the history of the borders of the State of Mississippi, the origins of the Public Land Survey System, how our state’s border history and the Public Land Survey System influences our modern day maps, and how to read, write and locate using the Public Land Survey System\.

title: Learning Objectives
text:
After completing the assigned readings, you should be able to:

- Understand the history of borders of the State of Mississippi
- Understand the history of the Public Land Survey System
- Define the components of the Public Land Survey System
- Identify and locate a parcel of land using this system

title: The History behind Mississippi’s Borders
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-124 - The History behind Mississippi’s Borders
text: The State of Mississippi inherited its current border from a few centuries worth of conquest and diplomacy\. In the age of discovery, European powers explored the world in search of new trading routes, wealth, and knowledge\. The Portuguese and Spanish were the first to dominate the exploration of the Americas, and the Spanish especially in North America\.

title: Early Exploration and Settlement
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-125 - Early Exploration and Settlement
text:
Hernando De Soto is credited with the first major Spanish expedition deep into the interior of the southeastern United States in 1539\. At this time, Spain had claimed Florida, Cuba, and much of the

Caribbean by discovery, exploration, and temporary occupancy\. De Soto was given the mission to conquer and occupy Florida\. After he did so, he then proceeded west through the southeastern United States, engaging in bloody battles with Native Americans all along his route\. Though his exact route is uncertain and debated, many scholars believe his route through Mississippi began near present\-day Lowndes County, proceeded north to Lee or Pontotoc County, and then turned west and crossing the Mississippi River in either DeSoto, Tunica, or Coahoma County\. De Soto’s excursion did not lead to broad Spanish settlement in the southeast, but instead lead the Spanish crown to concentrate its efforts in Florida, Cuba, and elsewhere\.

The French were next to explore the region, sailing south down the Wisconsin and Mississippi Rivers from their New France settlement in Canada\. In 1682, explorer Robert Cavalier de la Salle reached the mouth of the Mississippi River near present\-day Venice, Louisiana, and formally claimed the Mississippi River Valley in the name of King Louis XIV of France\. France’s primary goal was to establish a port on the Gulf of Mexico, which they did while securing a long navigable river along the way\. In the early 1700s, the French established settlements at Old Biloxi, Mobile, New Orleans, Baton Rouge, Natchez, and many other locations throughout the Mississippi River Valley, Ohio River Valley, and Great Lakes regions\.

The War of Spanish Succession, local skirmishes with Native Americans, and disease stifled the population growth of these early French settlements\. The economies of the French settlements also struggled, as most traders favored Spanish ports in the Gulf of Mexico causing a French trade monopoly to fail\. To make matters worse, the next trade monopoly was granted to John Law under the Mississippi Company, who exaggerated the riches of Louisiana\. Law issued hundreds of thousands of shares in the company and created a bubble that burst into hyperinflation, sharp increases in food prices, runs on his bank, and collapse of the company stock\. He eventually fled France, leaving his mess behind\.

Probably sensing weakness, the British established North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia and defined their western borders as the Mississippi River, thus claiming significant French territory for itself\. Intent on agitating the French in the region, the British armed the Chickasaws and supported their war efforts against the French\. Overall, the attempted French settlement of the south was largely a failure\.

title: British Dominion
text:
Mississippi came under new rule after the conclusion of the Seven Years War \(also called the French and Indian War\)\. In the Treaty of Paris 1763, Great Britain acquired the Mississippi River and all French territory lying east of the Mississippi River except for the town and island of New Orleans, which the French reserved for themselves\. By the same treaty, Spain ceded Florida to Great Britain in exchange for the return of Havana\. It was later revealed in 1764 that the remaining portion of French Louisiana west of the Mississippi River to the Rocky Mountains had been ceded to Spain under the Treaty of Fontainebleau – a secret treaty between France and Spain signed in 1762\.

Shortly after acquiring its new territory, the British divided its territory touching the Gulf of Mexico in the provinces of East and West Florida\. West Florida was defined as the portion of land west of the Chattahoochee River and east of the Mississippi River, bounded on the north by the 31st parallel and on the south by the Gulf of Mexico\. Today, the flat southern border of Mississippi and Alabama runs along the 31st parallel north\.

title: Post\-American Revolution
text:
The British dominion in Mississippi was short lived\. The United States issued its Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776 and Revolutionary War broke out\. During the war in the south, the Spanish, allied with the Americans, captured Natchez from its British royalist residents in 1779\. Under Don Bernardo de Galvez, the Spanish continued its conquest of British West Florida, capturing Baton Rouge, Mobile, and Pensacola, and with them, the entire province of West Florida\. When the Revolutionary War ended, Great

Britain ceded East and West Florida to Spain and recognized the land north of the 31st parallel north and east of the Mississippi River to as United States territory\.

title: Post\-American Revolution
text: )Image Source: “U\.S\. Central Change, July 4, 1776” by Golbez is licensed under [CC BY\-SA 4\.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/deed.en)\.

title: Post\-American Revolution
text: The Spanish claimed West Florida’s northern boundary was much farther north than the 31st parallel, so it held over in Natchez for a few years after the Revolutionary War\. Eventually, the United States and Spain agreed that the 31st parallel was the horizontal line of demarcation between West Florida and the United States in the Treaty of San Lorenzo of 1795 \(also called the Pinckney’s Treaty\)\. The Mississippi River was the vertical line of demarcation\.

title: Post\-American Revolution
text: )Image Source: “U\.S\. Central Change, May 12, 1784” by Golbez is licensed under [CC BY\-SA 4\.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/deed.en)\.

title: Yazoo Land Fraud
text:
Around the same time that the U\.S\. and Spain agreed that the 31st Parallel would become a common boundary, the Georgia legislature set its eyes on Mississippi land and committed what would later be called

the Yazoo Land Fraud\. Induced by bribes, in 1795, the Georgia legislature conveyed 35,000,000 acres of land in what is today the States of Alabama and Mississippi for a mere $500,000—less than $0\.02 per acre—to a handful of land speculation companies\.

title: Yazoo Land Fraud
text:
Image: Public Domain

Amid public outrage, one year later, a newly elected Georgia legislature tried to invalidate the grants by repealing the prior act, and in 1802, Georgia ceded all claims to land west of its current border to the United States\. By this time, however, much of the land had been resold to third parties\. The controversy reached the Supreme Court in the case of *Fletcher v\. Peck*, 10 U\.S\. 87 \(1810\)\. The Supreme Court held that subsequent bona fide purchasers had acquired good title to the Yazoo lands and their titles could not be abrogated by Georgia’s legislative actions—an unconstitutional infringement on a legal contract\. In 1814, Congress passed a law to address the outstanding claims\. The act provided a mechanism for claimants under the Yazoo sales to release their claims, assign them to the United States, and get paid out of the money generated from the sales of public lands\.

title: Mississippi Territory Established
text: While the Yazoo Land Fraud controversy was playing out, Congress established the Mississippi Territory in 1798\. Section three of the act defined the territories borders as bounded on the west by the Mississippi River, on the north by a line due east from the mouth of the Yazoo River \(Vicksburg\) to the Chattahoochee River, on the east by the Chattahoochee River, and on the south by the 31st parallel\. This 31st parallel, the line of demarcation between the Mississippi Territory and Spanish West Florida, was surveyed between 1798 and 1800 by Andrew Ellicott\.

title: Mississippi Territory Established
text: )Image Source: “U\.S\. Central Change, April 7, 1798” by Golbez is licensed under [CC BY\-SA 4\.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/deed.en)\.

title: Mississippi Territory Established
text: Due to the Yazoo Land Fraud, Congress authorized \([1 Stat\. 549](http://legisworks.org/sal/1/stats/STATUTE-1-Pg549a.pdf)\) President John Adams to appoint commissioners to negotiate with Georgia about ceding its western land\. Georgia ceded its western half, known as the Yazoo Lands, to the federal government\. At the same time, the federal government ceded to Georgia the eastern portion of the land previously ceded by South Carolina, though in reality Georgia technically already held title to the land, as the description of the earlier cession was based on an erroneous understanding of geography\.

title: Mississippi Territory Established
text: )Image Source: “U\.S\. Central Change, April 26, 1802” by Golbez is licensed under [CC BY\-SA 4\.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/deed.en)\.

title: Mississippi Territory Established
text:
On March 27, 1804, the land between Tennessee and Mississippi Territory previously ceded by Georgia was assigned to the Mississippi Territory\.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,

title: Mississippi Territory Established
text: )Image Source: “U\.S\. Central Change, March 27, 1804” by Golbez is licensed under [CC BY\-SA 4\.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/deed.en)\.

title: The Louisiana Purchase
text:
Although Spain possessed large tracts of territory in North and South America, its influence and control in the Americas was declining\. So too was its global power\. Fearing an American or European invasion into New Orleans and its land to the west, it retroceded Louisiana to France in 1800 by a secret treaty in exchange for territories in Tuscany, Italy\. It did so to establish a French barrier between the United States and its land further west\. The loss of Louisiana and Florida to the United States would give the United States a dominant and commanding presence over trade in the Gulf of Mexico\. Additionally, Spain hoped French Louisiana under the rule of Napoleon Bonaparte would deter an American invasion of its western territories\.

The United States heard about the secret treaty, and President Thomas Jefferson feared that Louisiana under French rule could potentially cut off the Mississippi River from American commerce\. He sent Robert Livingston and James Monroe to France to negotiate the purchase of New Orleans and free navigation of the Mississippi River\. They were surprised when Napoleon’s ministers offered the entire Louisiana territory to the United States\. Livingston and Monroe’s authority only extended to New Orleans and the Mississippi River, but they did not have time to get authority for the entire territory and began negotiations right away\. They secured a deal for the entire 828,000 square mile Louisiana territory for the equivalent of approximately $15 million dollars of US bonds and debt forgiveness\. Napoleon, in turn, sold the bonds at a discount and received only $8,831,250 in cash for Louisiana\. While Jefferson had authorized

$10 million dollars for only the City of New Orleans, he received a deal for only $5 million dollars more than doubled the size of the United States\.

title: The Louisiana Purchase
text: )Image Source: “U\.S\. Central Change, December 20, 1803” by Golbez is licensed under [CC BY\-SA 4\.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/deed.en)\.

title: Acquiring the coast
text:
After the Louisiana Purchase was completed, the United States claimed that the portion of Spanish West Florida located between the Mississippi River and the Perdido River was included in the purchase\. The Spanish regarded the claim as baseless\. However, the United States continued to press its claim and enacted legislation in 1804 that gave it the right to annex the territory, infuriating the Spanish\.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,

title: Acquiring the coast
text: )Image Source: “U\.S\. Central Change, December 20, 1803” by Golbez is licensed under [CC BY\-SA 4\.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/deed.en)\.

title: Acquiring the coast
text:
By 1810, European Spain was in a weak and fragile state and had lost influence over its colonies\. It was under the occupation of Napoleon at that time, who had declared his brother, Joseph, as King of Spain\. The United States did not want West Florida to fall into the hands of the British or Napoleon, so in 1810, the President directed the Governor of Orleans Territory to take possession of West Florida and hold it for the United States\. In 1812, Louisiana gained statehood and its eastern border was defined as the Pearl River\. In the same year, the remainder of West Florida was annexed to the Mississippi Territory\. In the Adams\-

Onis Treaty of 1819, Spain formally ceded both East and West Florida to the United States, ending its dominion over all territory east of the Mississippi River\.

title: Acquiring the coast
text:
Image Source: Public Domain

The claimed portion of West Florida east of the Pearl River was assigned to Mississippi Territory, though the area around Mobile Bay remained under the control of Spanish Florida\. The United States militarily occupied Mobile and the surrounding area up to the Perdido River in April 1813\.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,

title: Acquiring the coast
text: )Image Source: “U\.S\. Central Change, May 14, 1812” by Golbez is licensed under [CC BY\-SA 4\.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/deed.en)\.

title: Indian Treaties
text:
The northern portion of Mississippi was annexed in 1804\. Recall that the original northern border of the Mississippi Territory was a line due east from the junction of the Yazoo and Mississippi Rivers to the Chattahoochee River—roughly 32\.47 degrees north latitude\. The land north of this parallel was annexed in the 1804 act stemming from Georgia’s cession of its paper claims west to the Mississippi River\.

The Choctaw and Chickasaw Nations still inhabited present\-day North Mississippi at this time\. They ceded the remainder of their lands in multiple treaties\. The Choctaw Nation, through a series of treaties, beginning in 1801 and ending in 1831, ceded all their lands east of the Mississippi River to the United States\. The last cession treaty, the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek, ceded their remaining lands in exchange for land in present\-day Oklahoma\. It was the first removal treaty carried into effect under the Indian Removal Act\. The following map shows the Choctaw lands ceded by each treaty\.

title: Indian Treaties
text: The Chickasaw Nation ceded all its land in present\-day Mississippi in the Treaty of Pontotoc Creek of 1832\. This treaty was a renegotiation of an earlier treaty in 1830 that the Chickasaws refused to be bound by when they discovered the poor quality of the land they received\. The Chickasaw Nation eventually agreed to purchase some of the Choctaw’s new western land for $530,000 in the Treaty of Doaksville of 1837\. Under the Treaty of Pontotoc Creek, the Chickasaws were granted temporary homesteads of full sections of public lands, which they were authorized to convey in exchange for money\. They also received over $3 million for sales of unallotted land\. The Chickasaw Trail of Tears was the least traumatic among the five civilized tribes to make the journey\.

title: Mississippi Achieves Statehood
text:
In 1817, Congress enacted legislation providing for the formation of Mississippi and Alabama out of the Mississippi Territory\. The eastern border of Mississippi was the last portion of the state to receive a description\. The full description of the state border read:

“Beginning on the river Mississippi at the point where the southern boundary line of the state of Tennessee strikes the same, thence east along the said boundary line to the Tennessee river, thence up the same to the mouth of Bear Creek, thence by a direct line to the north\-west corner of the county of Washington, thence due south to the Gulf of Mexico, thence westwardly, including all the islands within six leagues of the shore, to the most eastern junction of Pearl river with Lake Borgne, thence up said river to the thirty\-first degree of north latitude, thence west along the said degree of latitude to the Mississippi river, thence up the same to the beginning\.”

title: Mississippi Achieves Statehood
text: )Image Source: “U\.S\. Central Change, March 3, 1817” by Golbez is licensed under [CC BY\-SA 4\.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/deed.en)\.

title: Mississippi Achieves Statehood
text: With this act, Mississippi had a definite border\. Its dynamic river boundaries have caused disputes between Mississippi and its neighbors throughout the years, but this original description is still valid today\. It is codified by reference to the 1817 act in Miss\. Code Ann\. § 3\-3\-1\.

title: Historical Development of the PLSS
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-134 - Historical Development of the PLSS
text:
Historically, the land was surveyed using the indiscriminate metes and bounds system\. This survey system used natural land features, such as trees and streams, as well as neighboring landowners, along with distances to describe plots of land\. Realizing that metes and bounds descriptions would never prove satisfactory in the largely uninhabited Northwest Territory \(what is now Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, and Wisconsin\), the Continental Congress knew it had to develop a plan for the orderly sale of individual tracts to the public\. In 1784, a committee headed by Thomas Jefferson developed a plan for dividing this public land into rectangles\. The new system was based on a series of coordinates – meridians and baselines – plotted astronomically by surveyors\.

The Continental Congress established the Public Land Survey System in the Land Ordinance of 1785, also known as the Northwest Ordinance\. Under terms of the ordinance, Congress was to appoint one surveyor from each state to serve under the direction of the geographer of the United States\.

The basic plan called for by Jefferson’s committee developed three theories:

1. the principal of “survey before settlement”;
2. the principal of a mathematically designed plan to be followed throughout the entire public domain area;
3. the creation of a standard land unit, the section of uniform shape and area and with boundaries physically marked on the ground\.

The Land Act of May 18, 1796, was the first law concerning surveys\. The act created the office of Surveyor General and established the method by which townships are subdivided\. The act delegated the authority to write surveying rules and regulations to the Surveyor General\. These top\-level officials were all

technically and scientifically oriented and advanced for their time\. Their goal was to ensure that the surveys of the public lands would be systematic and rigorously executed\.

When the Mississippi Territory was established in 1798, the territory already had settlers—most of which received large land grants from either the British or Spanish Governments\. The Land Act of March 3, 1803 \(2 Stat\. 229\) enabled these residents to be confirmed in their claims under the prior grants and directed these lands to be surveyed\. The act also provided for the establishment of two land offices, registers and receivers, a board of land commissioners to settle private land claims, and a system for recording claims\. Further, this act established the office of Surveyor of Lands South of Tennessee and directed all lands for which Indian titles had to be extinguished to be surveyed\. At this time, surveyors were paid based on the number of miles surveyed, capped at a maximum of $4 per mile\.

In 1803, the US Surveyor General ordered work to begin by running a meridian line from a monument on the 31st parallel north to the then\-Indian boundary and laying out townships\. The Surveyor of the Lands South of Tennessee, however, was concerned about fitting the private claims into the Townships and Range format\. His concern was fitting irregular parcels into a structured rectangular system, causing the same parcel to flow into multiple townships and breaking the section numbering system\. Nevertheless, these parcels were labeled sections and were assigned a number, causing some townships to have over 100 sections, resulting in a great deal of confusion later\.

The Land Act of March 26, 1804 \(2 Stat\. 277\) was the first major act affecting the public land surveys after the surveys were extended to the Mississippi Territory\. Among other things, this act provided for:

- 
	- Extension of the US Surveyor General’s authority to all the lands north of the Ohio and east of the Mississippi River, to which Indian title had been extinguished or “shall hereafter be extinguished;”
	- Reservation of section 16 for schools, three townships for a college, and salt springs;
	- Land sales and patenting procedures;
	- Public lands to be offered for sale in half sections or in quarter sections; and
	- The division of surveyed lands into surveying districts, and appointment of a district surveyor, who was to subdivide the lands in his district into sections, half sections, and quarter sections\.

title: Historical Development of the PLSS
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-134 - Historical Development of the PLSS
text:
The Land Act of March 26, 1804 \(2 Stat\. 283\) divided the Louisiana Purchase into the Territory of Orleans and the District of Louisiana\. The land south of the Mississippi Territory and south of the 33rd parallel, west of the Mississippi River were named Orleans Territory\.

The Land Act of March 27, 1804 \(2 Stat\. 303\) added the Georgia cession lands to the Mississippi Territory and extended the public land surveys to the additional territory\. The figure below indicates the boundaries of the Mississippi and Orleans Territories as they were claimed by the United States after the passage of this act\.

title: Historical Development of the PLSS
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-134 - Historical Development of the PLSS
text:
The Land Act of February 11, 1805 \(2 Stat\. 313\) crystallized the principles of the Public Land Survey System\. The act is codified in Chapter 18 of Title 43 of the United States Code and is still law\. The Act settled several basic principles of the subdivision of townships and sections:

- Corners and lines established by the United States survey are to be held as correct and proper corners and lines\. No subsequent survey can correct the corner position to place it more in conformity with the plan of survey\.
- After an original survey, subdivisions are to be made by connecting opposite corners with straight lines\. The method of quartering surveyed rectangular parcels such as sections is to connect the midpoint corners on opposite sides of the figure\.
- Where no such opposite corners exist, boundaries shall be made by running from established corners in a cardinal direction\. Fractional sections and quarter sections, that do not have an opposite side midpoint, are to be subdivided by running cardinal\.
- The corners of half and quarter sections, not marked by the original survey, shall be placed as nearly as possible equidistant from the two corners which stand on the same line\. Quarter\-section corners and other corners such as sixteenth\-section corners, which were not established by the federal survey, are to be established at the midpoint\.
- The acreage returned by United States survey shall be considered as exact\. Acreages shown on the plat of survey are to be used for land dispositions and apportionment of unsurveyed corners\.

The Land Act of March 2, 1805 \(2 Stat\. 324\) extended the authority of the Surveyor of Lands South of Tennessee to cover all the Mississippi and Orleans Territories and extended the system of rectangular surveys to cover all the lands in those territories\.

In an 1815 letter to Surveyor of the Lands South of Tennessee, the General Land Office \(“GLO”\) Commissioner said he was “astonished” to hear that the deputy surveyors had not marked bearing trees at the survey corners in approximately 30 townships\. The first Surveyor of the Lands South of Tennessee had not instructed them to mark trees, only to set posts at the corners and to mark the post because of the impossibility of correctly numbering the sections in a township containing private claims as the survey progresses\. Each private claim whether large or small would have a separate number, so a township may contain any number of sections, sometimes over 100\. The proper number could not be ascertained until the

survey was complete\. The surveyor would then retravel over his lines with his map, and transfer the proper sectional number from it to the corner trees, or posts, of sections\.

This policy of identifying private land claims as sections was unusual and unnecessary\. It is unknown how long this mode of identifying private claims continued\. In the north, the claims were given numbers but separately identified from the rectangular sections\. The lack of a definite policy and common instructions for all public land surveys was evident and needed correction\. The problem can be seen in map of T11N R2E, Washington Meridian, Mississippi:

title: Historical Development of the PLSS

text:
On March 1, 1817, Congress passed the Mississippi Enabling Act \(3 Stat\. 348\), with the boundaries of the new State described as they exist today\. Mississippi was admitted to the Union on December 10, 1817\. On March 3, 1817, Congress created the Territory of Alabama \(3 Stat\. 371\), with boundaries as they are today, from what was left of the former Mississippi Territory\. The Alabama Enabling Act \(3 Stat\. 489\) was passed two years later in 1819, and the Mississippi Alabama border was surveyed less than a year later\.

In 1821, survey work began on the land ceded by the Choctaw Nation in the Treaty of Doak’s Stand\. Surveyors established the initial point at the intersection of the Choctaw Meridian and Baseline in the same year\. Work began on the south boundary of the land ceded and extended northerly\.

In 1823, the GLO Commissioner wrote to the head surveyor in Washington, Mississippi regarding the first instance where a fraudulent meander was found in a Mississippi survey\. The township concerned was T14N R5E, Washington Meridian, through which the Big Black River meanders south of Vicksburg, Mississippi\. The Big Black River was, in fact, much further north than the original plat showed\. As a result, the GLO Commissioner gave blanket permission to the local office to execute resurveys whenever it was “satisfied that it is of importance to the public interest to have resurveys made\.” The ramifications of such authority caused many problems and litigation in the years ahead, given that many parcels had already been entered or patented\. The most famous case in this area is probably the case of *Cragin vs\. Powell*, 128 U\.S\. 691, a Louisiana case decided by the U\.S\. Supreme Court in 1888\.

Later in 1823, the GLO Commissioner ordered the head surveyors in the Mississippi and Alabama districts to accurately connect the township and section lines against the state line between Alabama and

Mississippi, showing the fractions of sections made fractional by the state line\. For background, the St\. Stephens Meridian survey district is located in both states\. The township and section lines had been run before the boundary was surveyed in 1820, and the boundary survey had not tied in the section lines\. A question arose as to what part of a section should be taxed by the State of Alabama and what part by Mississippi\. After the Illinois\-Indiana line caused similar and expensive problems, it was decided that the rectangular surveys would be held in abeyance until after these sections were tied to the state line\.

In 1826, the GLO Commissioner directed local offices to make 80\-acre subdivisions of sections by either a north\-south or east\-west line in fractional sections against water boundaries where there were at least 80\-acres\. The remainder was left as fractional lots\. The result was that there were many more small fractions left after the full half\-quarter section was designated\. For example, the “E 1/2 SW l/4 Sec\. 19” may have 80 acres, while the west half of this quarter section may have 38 acres or maybe only five\. This definition of fractional section and the lotting procedure was used by GLO Commissioners until 1832\.

In 1831, the GLO Commissioner directed the head surveyor of Mississippi lands to prepare written instructions for his deputies\. These were issued under the title, “Instructions for Surveying the Lands of the United States, in the State of Mississippi\.” Among other things, these instructions directed townships to be subdivided by erecting half\-mile posts for quarter\-section corners\. Unfortunately, many of the half\-mile posts were not quarter\-section corners because they were not established according to the law\. Seeming to enact its own code, these instructions also introduced bark scribing of bearing trees and numerous other changes in methods\.

text:
In 1833, surveys were ordered for the land ceded by the Chickasaws in northern Mississippi under the Treaty of Pontotoc Creek of 1832\. These surveys were ordered three years earlier upon news of an earlier treaty with the Chickasaws, but the Chickasaws refused to move to the lands assigned to them under that treaty as they found them unacceptable\. They renegotiated, and the surveys were stalled\. Under the original plan, the Chickasaw lands were to be surveyed as an extension of the Choctaw surveys\. But plans changed and a separate office for these surveys was set up in Pontotoc, Mississippi and work began on establishing the Chickasaw Meridian\. This change in plans created a fifth meridian system for Mississippi surveys, making Mississippi second only to Ohio in complexity\.

The initial point of the Chickasaw Meridian was established in 1833 on the east bank of the Wolf River and on the south boundary of Tennessee\. The field notes from these surveys indicate that the State boundary used was run by “General Winchester” in 1819, and it appears he missed the mark by roughly three miles to the north\. Nevertheless, the point was fixed and from that point, the basis meridian for the Chickasaw surveys was extended due south\. This erroneous State line causes sections one through 18 to fall in the State of Tennessee for many townships just south of the baseline\.

Although the goal of the rectangular survey system was to provide a consistent and reliable method of describing public lands, in practice the procedures used sometimes fell short\. For instance, in 1834, the GLO Commissioner suggested that the Mississippi Surveyor General adjust his platting procedure for private claims\. The then\-current practice was to designate private claims tracts as a distinct section\. But the commissioner suggested a scheme that would require resurveying the township into regular sections and surveying the private claims as lots within the sections where the tracts fell\. The renumbering and resurveying of all these sections seemed unreasonable to the Mississippi Surveyor General so he only designated the private claims as lots, leaving the section numbering scheme in place\. Presumably, the fractions of the sections lying outside the claims would have been given lot numbers, but it appears they were not\.

Between 1851 and 1855 the Land Act was amended several times and set the pattern for the present\-day survey system\. Later, the Land Act of July 9, 1870, codified in 43 U\.S\.C\. § 766, for the first time officially allowed county and local surveyors to subdivide surveyed public land\. In practice, they had been subdividing sections since much earlier\.

Numerous “Manuals of Surveying Instructions” have been published over the years by the GLO and its successor, the Bureau of Land Management\. The Public Land Survey System, as we know it today, is a system based on tiered townships and ranges that are tied to 37 established principal meridians located across the country\. Many of the laws regarding the survey of public lands enacted between 1805 and 1870 have since been codified in Title 43, Chapter 18 of the United States Code:

United States Code Title 43 \- Public Lands \- Chapter 18 \- Survey of Public Lands [43 U\.S\. Code § 751](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/43/751)\. Rules of survey \[Derived from Act Feb\. 11, 1805\]\.

[43 U\.S\. Code § 752](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/43/752)\. Boundaries and contents of public lands; how ascertained \[Derived from Act Feb\. 11, 1805\]\.

[43 U\.S\. Code § 753](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/43/753)\. Lines of division of half quarter sections; how run \[Derived from Acts Apr\. 24, 1820 and Apr\. 5, 1832\]\.

title: Initial Points
text: The structure of the rectangular system of survey is simple\. The entire system was built around __initial points__\. When entering a new, unsurveyed area, the surveyor would establish an initial point from which to begin the survey\. The surveyor defined the initial point by determining the exact latitude and longitude through astronomical observations or through ties to other points known geographical position\. Unfortunately, it wasn’t until around 1902 that surveyors began using indestructible monuments, usually by copper bolts firmly set in a rock ledge when possible and witnessed by rock bearings\. In all, thirty\-seven initial points have been set throughout the United States\.

title: Initial Points
text:
Mississippi was defined by several surveys, and there are three \(3\) initial points within its borders\. This is because treaties settling land claims in this region, from conflicts with Indians and Spanish, came at different times\.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,

title: Initial Points
text: )Image Source: [Initial Point of the Choctaw Meridian](http://www.clui.org/section/choctaw-meridian) by The Center for Land Use Interpretation is licensed under [CC BY\-NC\-SA 3\.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/3.0/)\.

title: Initial Points
text: The initial point of the Choctaw Meridian was re\-established for historical purposes by a group of organizations including the Bureau of Land Management, Mississippi State University, and the Mississippi Association of Professional Surveyors \(M\.A\.P\.S\.\)\. A brass medallion sits in a granite disc embedded in a substantial amount of concrete at and below ground\.

title: Principal Meridian
text:
With the initial point established, surveyors would then establish a north\-south line configured from __true north __\(not magnetic north\) extending to the limits of the area to be covered\. The north\-south line that intersects the initial point is called the __principal meridian__\. This line of longitude was used as a starting point and reference for all sectionalized land\.

![](data:image/png;base64,

title: Principal Meridian
text: The principal meridian is the principal north\-south line used for survey control in a large region, and which divides townships between east and west\.

title: Baselines
text: From the initial point, a line was extended east and/or west as a true parallel of latitude to the limits of the area to be covered\. The east\-west line that intersects the initial point is called the __baseline__\. Baselines are actually circular curves on the Earth’s surface\. A __latitude line __is an east\-west circle, measuring degrees north or south of the Equator\. A __longitude line __is a north\-south circle measuring degrees east and west of zero longitude at Greenwich, England\.

title: Baselines
text:
In Mississippi, there are three baselines and reference to five principal meridians\. The most prominent meridian is the Choctaw Meridian, which was established in 1821 and governs the surveys in most of central Mississippi\. The initial point for the Choctaw Meridian exists at the intersection of the Choctaw Baseline\. This baseline runs east and west through central Mississippi\. The initial point at the intersection of the Choctaw Meridian and Choctaw Baseline was forgotten and unmarked for over 150 years until it was re\-dedicated in 1998\.

The northern part of Mississippi was surveyed off the Chickasaw Meridian, whose Initial Point is uncertain, as records conflict about which baseline was actually used \(e\.g\., the unnamed baseline\)\. It is possible that the baseline was actually as much as 3 miles over the state line in Tennessee, due to previous surveying errors in that state \(Tennessee, like most of the mid\-southern and the northeastern states, was not a Public Land Survey state\), though the east/west state line between Mississippi and Tennessee is another possibility\. Some of the original surveys mark the state line in T1S\. Either way, no monument or marker has ever been found, despite hours of searching in swamps, and no plaques or signage have been erected\. This may be the least considered Initial Point in the lower 48 states\.

The Washington Meridian line was surveyed and established in 1803 by surveyor Isaac Briggs\. Briggs named the meridian the Washington Meridian, likely because the meridian passed near his offices in the community of Washington, Mississippi\. The Washington Meridian runs north from the St\. Stephen’s Baseline, which serves as both the Mississippi–Louisiana border and the Alabama and Florida border\. This baseline is the 31st\-degree latitude, and was originally established to separate the Spanish possessions in Florida from the territory of the United States\. \(Note: This boundary line was surveyed by Andrew Ellicott – hence, it is known as “Ellicott’s Corner”\)\.

The Washington Meridian is the basis of cadastral surveys in southwestern Mississippi, south of the Choctaw Meridian baseline and west of the territory of the Saint Stephens Meridian\. The Saint Helena Meridian is the basis for surveys in Louisiana east of the Mississippi River\. The location of the Washington Meridian line and Saint Helena Meridian line is unique, as it is actually two initial points in one place – the St\. Stephen’s Baseline; the Washington Meridian, extending north from the baseline into southern Mississippi in 1803, and the St\. Helena Meridian, heading south into Louisiana from the same point on the baseline in 1819\. This one is also unusual, as not only has the original marker never been discovered, but no commemorative marker has ever been erected for it\. It is one of the forgotten—or at least neglected—Initial Points\.

The Saint Stephens meridian, begins at the initial point \(Ellicott’s Corner\), on the baseline, passes through Saint Stephens, Alabama, extends south to Mobile Bay and then north, and governs the surveys in the southern district of Alabama, and in Pearl River district lying east of the river and south of the Choctaw Baseline, in the state of Mississippi\.

The Huntsville meridian, which begins on the northern boundary of Alabama and extends south, governs the surveys in the northern district of Alabama and a small portion of northeastern Mississippi\.

Once we know the meridian and the baseline for a property, we can determine the general location of any property anywhere in the country governed by the Public Land Survey System\.

title: Standard Parallels \(Correction Lines\)
text: Another major control in the structure of the rectangular system is the establishment of __standard parallels__\. Standard parallels extend true east and west, generally at intervals of 24 miles to the north and to the south of the baseline\. The first horizontal line to the north of the baseline is called the “1st Standard Parallel North,” and the next successive line north is called the “2nd Standard Parallel North,” and so forth\. The first horizontal line to the south of the baseline is called the “1st Standard Parallel South,” and so forth\. The following diagram is a generalized representation of the 24\-mile square pattern\.

title: Standard Parallels \(Correction Lines\)
text:
Each of the squares in the diagram represents a 24\-mile square tract or an area of 576 square miles \(not 24 square miles\)\. Additional guide meridians may exist to the east and west, and additional standard parallels may exist to the north and south, depending on the control needed for further surveys\.

Auxiliary guide meridians or auxiliary standard parallels are established and named when the intervals exceed the distance of 24 miles\.

title: Guide Meridians
text:
Because of the shape of the earth, principal meridians come closer together as they extend toward the North Pole\. If not corrected, a township on the baseline would be larger than one further north\. To adjust for this problem, correction lines called __guide meridians __are established\.

![](data:image/png;base64,

title: Guide Meridians
text: Guide Meridians extend true north and south, generally at intervals of 24 miles to the east and to the west of the principal meridian\. The vertical lines to the east or west of the principal meridian are known by either a name or a number, such as “1st Guide Meridian East” or “1st Guide Meridian West,” or “2nd Guide Meridian West,” and others\.

title: Township Lines and Range Lines
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-141 - Township Lines and Range Lines
text: __Township lines __were established at intervals of 6 miles to the north and 6 miles to the south of the baseline\. The resulting 6\-mile\-wide spaces are called townships and are numbered north and south of the baseline\. Remember that the spaces, not the lines, are called townships, and the spaces, not the lines, are numbered\. The first township north is called Township 1 North\. The next township north is called Township 2 North, and so on\.

title: Township Lines and Range Lines
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-141 - Township Lines and Range Lines
text: __Range lines __are established at intervals of 6 miles to the east and 6 miles to the west of the principal meridian\. The resulting 6\-mile\-wide spaces are called ranges and are numbered east and west of the principal meridian\. The first range west is called Range 1 West, the next range west is called Range 2 West, and so on\.

title: Townships and Ranges
text:
The range lines and the township lines intersect and establish the boundaries for 6\-mile by 6\-mile squares called townships\. Each township is identified by a unique description based on the principal meridian governing it\. Townships are identified by their number north or south of the baseline, followed by the number east or west of the principal meridian\.

![](data:image/png;base64,

title: Townships and Ranges
text:
Each township is 6 miles by 6 miles, or 36 square miles in size \(6 miles square\)\. In the above figure, the township’s location would be described as follows: Township 3 South, Range 3 West\. Abbreviated, this becomes T3S, R3W\.

The term “township” may be used to describe two different situations\. First, a __township __may be used to describe a series of 6\-mile\-wide horizontal rows north and south of the baseline\. These horizontal rows serve as the north\-south coordinates in the rectangular system of a cadastral survey\. The east\-west coordinates are the ranges\. Second, a __township __may be used to describe a single 6\-mile square area that is situated within two adjacent range lines and two adjacent township lines\.

The numbering of townships and ranges begins at the initial point of a principal meridian and a baseline\. Township numbers increase away from the baseline using the direction from the baseline as an indicator \(north or south\)\. Range numbers increase away from a principal meridian using the direction from the principal meridian as an indicator \(east or west\)\.

The township identified with the arrow in the below figure is 3 townships south of the baseline and 2 ranges east of the principal meridian\. Thus, it is described as follows: Township 3 South, Range 2 East\. Abbreviated, this becomes T3S, R2E\.

title: Sections
text:
A __section __is a one\-mile square block of land containing 640 acres\. There are 36 sections within each township\. Any correction to the size of the township due to measuring error occurs along the western or northern side\. As a result, the sections along the western or northern side of the township may not equal one\-mile square\.

![](data:image/png;base64,

title: Sections
text: The sections in each township are always numbered consecutively, beginning with the number 1 in the northeast corner of the township, and counting westerly six sections; then, with the number 7, south of section 6, counting back to the east side of the township, and so on, weaving back and forth through the sections of the township, and ending with number 36 in the southeast corner\.

title: Fractional Townships
text:
There are also half townships and half ranges that do not contain all 36 square miles\. In some areas, there are one\-quarter and three\-quarter townships and ranges\. These townships or ranges are referred to as __fractional townships__\.

![](data:image/png;base64,

title: Fractional Townships
text: Fractional townships occur because of irregularities in the survey because the township is intersected by a state, reservation, or grant boundary or by a large body of water\. The above figure is an example of a fractional township resulting from the boundary line between lands located in the Choctaw and Chickasaw districts\.

title: Fractional Sections
text:
In sections made fractional by rivers, lakes, or other bodies of water, lots are formed bordering on the body of water and numbered consecutively through the section\. Boundaries of lots usually follow the quarter section and quarter\-quarter section lines\. However, surveyors tried to avoid extreme lengths or narrow widths and areas with fewer than 5 acres or more than 45 acres\.

![](data:image/png;base64,

title: Fractional Sections
text:
The above figure is an example of a fractional township resulting from the shoreline of a body of water\. The sections of land abutting the body of water \(Sections 4, 5, 8, 9, 16, 17 and 18\) are called fractional sections\.

Quarter sections along the north and west boundaries of a township made irregular by discrepancies of measures and convergence of the range lines, are usually numbered as lots\. Lot lines are not actually run in the field\. Like quarter\-section lines, they are merely indicated on the plats\. Areas need for selling the lots are computed from the plats\.

title: Monuments
text: __Monuments __were required to be set at each mile at section corners\. A monument is also set between each section corner\. These monuments are called __quarter section corners __and are set so that a section can be subdivided into quarters\. __Boundaries __for the Public Land Survey System were usually marked by placing markers or using prominent trees as boundary markers\. These boundary markers are referred to as monuments\. Monuments are tangible landmarks indicating boundaries\. There are 5 different types of monuments\. A __physical monument __is an existing feature such as a stone or stake but not the line of an adjoining property\. A __natural monument __is a naturally occurring object such as a lake, river, tree, boulder, or hill\. An __artificial monument __is a man\-made object such as a stake, fence, set stone, etc\. A __record monument __is an adjoining property called for in a deed such as a street or a particular parcel of land\. Finally, a __legal monument __is any monument referenced in a legal description for the purposes of identifying property\.

title: Subdivisions
text:
-

			1. __Aliquot Parts__

__Aliquot __is a Latin word meaning to divide \(a number or quantity\) into equal\-parts leaving no remainder\. In legal descriptions, only quarter or half divisions of a section of land are known as __aliquot parts__\. An aliquot part is always described in relation to the four points of the compass, with the use of the standard compass abbreviations, N, W, S, E\.

title: Subdivisions
text: For example, to describe the west half of a section, you write “W1/2”; the east half would be written as “E1/2\.” The same rule applies to the north and south half, “N1/2” and “S1/2” respectively, as shown in the figure below\. To describe each of the quarter\-sections, you need to add one notation; that is, show which of the four quarters is intended, such as “NE1/4,” or “NW1/4,” or “SW1/4,” or “SE1/4\.”

title: Subdivisions
text: In describing adjoining quarter sections, combine NE1/4 and NW1/4 to make N1/2 or combine SW1/4 and SE1/4 to make S1/2\. The “1/2” and the “1/4” are the only fractions that appear in the description of land by aliquot parts\. The figure below shows a section divided into several parcels of land\. The letters A, B, and C are used to identify some of the parcels\.

title: Half Section
text:
Parcel C, the west half of the section, would be written as W1/2\. Parcel C may also be referred to as a half\-section\. To describe parcel B, which is the east half of the west half, write E1/2 W1/2\.

Whenever describing a parcel of land within another parcel of land, always write the smaller parcel to the left of the larger parcel\.

title: Quarter Section
text: Suppose you want to describe the northeast quarter of the section shown below\. Describe the northeast quarter as NE1/4\. Since the northeast quarter represents one fourth of the section, it is called a quarter section\. To describe the southwest quarter of that quarter section, write SW1/4 NE1/4\.

title: Quarter\-Quarter Section
text:
To describe the southwest quarter of that quarter section, write SW1/4 NE1/4\.

In the diagram below, the dark line is the boundary of the NE1/4\. The shaded area shows the SW1/4 within the NE1/4, which is described as SW1/4 NE1/4\.

![](data:image/png;base64,

title: Acreages
text:
When writing an aliquot part description of a section, begin in the most northeastern portion and work in a counter\-clockwise direction, regardless of where the largest portion is located\. Perhaps we should take a moment here to look at the size in acres, of the land we are learning to describe\. Generally, a section of land consists of 640 acres, but sections along the north and west boundaries of a township will not generally contain 640 acres because of the convergence of meridians\.

A quarter section such as the northeast quarter \(NE1/4\) would consist of 160 acres \(1/4 of 640 acres\)\. A quarter\-quarter section such as the southwest quarter of the northeast quarter \(SW1/4 NE1/4\) would consist of 40 acres\. A further quartering of the SW1/4 NE1/4 parcel would result in four parcels of 10 acres each\.

title: Acreages
text: An entire section of land equals 640 acres\.

title: Minor Subdivisions
text: The subdivisions of sections into 10 and 5\-acre parcels follow the same rule you have already learned\. Remember that when you describe a parcel of land within another parcel of land, the smaller parcel is always written to the left of the larger parcel\. With each subdivision, the legal description grows longer and to the left\.

title: The Comma
text: The inadvertent omission or insertion of a comma can be very misleading and can significantly impact the accuracy of a land description\. Commas in land descriptions mean “AND THE,” whereas the absence of commas means “OF THE\.” To show the effect of a comma \(or commas\) in a land description, let’s take a typical description of a 10\-acre parcel\. The notation SW1/4 __*of the *__NW1/4 __*of the *__NE1/4 is read as “the southwest quarter northwest quarter northeast quarter\.”

title: The Comma
text:
By inserting a single comma into the notation between SW1/4 and NW1/4 we have drastically changed the notation\.

![](data:image/png;base64,

title: The Comma
text:
Instead of describing a single 10\-acre parcel, we are now describing two separate parcels totaling 200 acres \(160 acres and 40 acres respectively\)\. The notation would now be read as “the southwest quarter __*and the *__northwest quarter __*of the *__northeast quarter\.”

![](data:image/png;base64,

title: Lots
text:
__Lots __are irregular or fractional parts of land in a section that cannot be described as aliquot parts\. They generally lie on the north and the west sides of a township, or along meandering lakes, ponds, or rivers\. That lots are created as a result of irregularities in boundaries or resurveys presents unusual problems, which are beyond the scope of the self\-study guide\.

Be aware, however, that lots exist, that they serve a purpose in the rectangular system of survey, and that they generally are numbered by the same method as are sections\. The following example will show how lots are numbered and will help you to visualize some of the circumstances that result in lotting\.

title: Lots
text: In the above example, the north and west side of the section contains fractional parcels of land ranging in size from 36\.70 acres to 41\.20 acres\. Because these parcels cannot be described as aliquot parts, they cannot be considered as quarter\-quarter sections\. Hence, they are described as lots\. Note that the lots are numbered consecutively from east to west and then from north to south\.

title: Lost Corners
text: Although a United States government section corner is the official corner of a section, monuments located and placed by the original government surveyors on these corners may have been lost or obliterated\. Even if the title to a section of land is clear of any defect affecting the marketability of the parcel, if one or more of the corners have disappeared, the lost marker must be reestablished and accepted by the surveyors in the area as the correct location, or the matter must be established through litigation\.

title: Bent Section Lines
text: It is not unusual to find that some section lines in the original government surveys actually bend\. That is, the line will have two or more different bearings along its length\. The existence of “bent” section lines can be discovered only by reference to those original governmental surveys\. When discovered, further inquiry is almost always required to eliminate the possibility of overlap or other title dispute arising from the occupation of the land and its conformity to the record title\. Although original government surveys may contain bent lines, subsequent private surveys establishing fractional sections within government sections may not contain bent lines\.

title: Irregular Sections
Mistakes In Descriptions
text:
Mistakes in fractional section descriptions are frequently made, and complex descriptions are often difficult to follow even if there is no mistake\. For example, a careless drafter may substitute “southwest”

when “southeast” is intended\. When the title is reviewed, the same error can be made or overlooked, thereby continuing and compounding the error\. Careful proofreading is required\.

Several methods may be used to minimize errors that occur when using a fractional section description\. One is to draw out the description on a section map and use this as a reference throughout the examination of the title\. This constant reminder will minimize mistakes and is a good way to save time because the description does not have to be recreated in the mind of the examiner as the examination progresses\.

title: Reading PLSS Descriptions
text:
A strength of the Public Land Survey System is that the land has been, for the most part, divided evenly\. This makes property descriptions more uniform and predictable\. Under the Public Land Survey System, land can be described in one of three ways\. When locating these parcels, the descriptions are read backward to specifically locate the property\.

__Fractional__:	Describing property using fractions of rectangles\. For example: E1/2, NE1/4, Section 6, Township 3 North, Range 4 West\.

__Acreage__:	Describing property using the acreage values associated with each fraction of a rectangle\. For example:

West 80 acres, NE1/4 Section 6, Township 3 North, Range 4 West\.

__Lineal__:	Describing property using the perimeter measurement of each fraction of a rectangle\.

For example:

The East 400 feet of the Southeast Quarter of Section 7, Township 2 South, Range 1 East\.

The following figure shows how an individual section of the Public Land Survey System can be dissected using land descriptions in order to describe the property\. The diagram shows section divisions and land measurements\. A section is simply a large square that is one mile from east to west and one mile from north to south\.

The large square, or section, can be divided into four equal parts creating the Northeast Quarter, the Northwest Quarter, the Southeast Quarter and the Southwest Quarter of the entire section\.

Considering an entire section is 640 acres, by dividing the section by four \(quartering the section\), each quarter section is 160 acres \(640 ÷ 4 = 160\)\. Therefore, if a property is described as the NW1/4 section, the total acreage of that property is 160 acres\. Property can be further divided into a quarter\-quarter section\. If the property is described as the NW1/4 of the NW1/4, the section has been quartered twice \(640 ÷ 4 = 160 ÷ 4 = 40\); the property contains 40 acres\. This division by one\-fourth can continue to a quarter\-quarter\-quarter which would contain 10 acres, and a quarter\-quarter\-quarter\-quarter containing 2\.5 acres\. Tracts smaller than 2\.5 acres are generally described using the metes and bounds description\.

Property can be dissected using any combination of fractional portions\. For example, a single parcel can be the equivalent of one half of a section, or 320 acres\. The half section can be the north half or the south half or the east half or west half\.

title: Locating Fractional Interests
text: When locating legal descriptions that are fractional \(NE1/4 of the NW1/4 of the SE1/4\), begin with the whole 640 acres of the section\. Go to the end of the legal description for the last part of the section\. In this example, the last part mention is “SE1/4\.” Divide the section into 4 equal parts \(since the SE1/4 is described\)\. Each part is 160 acres \(640 acres in a section divided by 4\)\. Now locate the SE1/4 on the grid\.

text:
When locating legal descriptions that are by acreage \(W 10 acres of the NW1/4 of the SE1/4\), begin with the whole 640 acres of the section\.

![](data:image/png;base64,

title: Locating Acreage
text:
__Step 1__:

![](data:image/png;base64,

title: Locating Acreage
text:
__Step 2__:

Locate the West 10 acres of the NW1/4 of the SE1/4

This NW1/4 of the SE1/4 contains 40 acres\. 640 acres ÷ 4 ÷ 4 = 40 acres\. The legal description calls for the west 10 acres of this\. These 10 acres will be on the west side of the 40 acres\.

title: Locating Linear Measurement
text:
When locating legal descriptions that are by linear measurement \(E 10 chains off of the NW1/4 of the SE1/4\), begin with the whole 640 acres of the section\.

![](data:image/png;base64,

title: Locating Linear Measurement
text:
__Step 1__:

Locate the NW1/4 of the SE1/4 as in the previous example, which is 40 acres\.

![](data:image/png;base64,

title: Locating Linear Measurement
text:
__Step 2__:

Since the legal calls for the east 10 chains, locate the east side \(marked with a thicker line\)\.

__Step 3__:

Make a horizontal line from the NE corner, of the part that has already been identified, west 10 chains \(660’\)\.

__Step 4__:

Make a horizontal line from the SE corner, of the part that has already been identified, west 10 chains \(660’\)\.

title: Locating Linear Measurement
text:
__Step 5__:

Connect the endpoints of the lines representing the 10 chains to make a rectangle\.

title: Overview
text: This chapter covers the drawing of metes and bounds legal descriptions\. The purpose of this chapter is to provide a detailed understanding of how to describe real property using the metes and bounds system\.

title: Learning Objectives
text:
After completing the assigned readings in this chapter, you should be able to:

- Understand the components of a metes and bounds description
- Recognize the tools used to plot a description
- Read and draw parcels from a metes and bounds legal description
