title: Historical Development
text:
Centuries ago a buyer and seller would walk the perimeter of a tract and observe the monuments or place new ones and consummate the transfer with the seller picking up a stone or twig from the land and handing it to the buyer\. Later they would describe the land in a document and walk the lines\. The walking and transfer of objects from the lands involved what was called the action of __livery of seizin__\. It was common in England but was not continued by the colonists of the new world\.

Originally, adjacent landowners, trees, rocks, rivers, traveled ways, and so forth were used to describe the perimeter of the property\. These physical features defining the boundary were the “__bounds__” portion of the metes and bounds description\. With the development of better equipment that reduced cost, the evolution of surveying techniques, and the desire of the public to more accurately define what they were doing, the addition of the “metes” portion to the metes and bounds description became feasible\. The term “__metes__” refers to segment measurements of a boundary, specified by a distance between the terminal points, and orientation or direction\. A direction may be a simple compass bearing or a precise orientation determined by accurate survey methods\. By the time of the break with England, the metes and bounds description was prevalent in, what was to become, the United States\.

The system of metes and bounds is and was used to survey and describe the land in the original thirteen colonies, Kentucky, Texas, West Virginia, Tennessee, Maine, Hawaii and parts of Ohio\. Corners were usually artificial landmarks not of a permanent character—trees, stumps, bends in creeks, etc\.—which tended to disappear or change over a time span of several generations\. Items of a permanent nature were seldom used and the surveyor and mapper’s notes of a survey of the land were often incomplete\. People simply didn’t have the concept of permanence in their minds as far as descriptions were concerned\. They knew what they were transferring and that was as far as their minds would carry it\. Also, while considerably better than earlier equipment, the surveying equipment of the time was less than accurate\.

In the eastern United States, individuals first acquired land titles by gift or purchase from the European governments that were trying to establish colonies\. Surveys and maps were either lacking or inadequately made, and descriptions could be given only in general terms\. The remaining land in the thirteen colonies was transferred to the states at the close of the Revolutionary War\. Later, this land was parceled out to individuals, usually in irregular tracts\.

Many original transfers and subsequent ownership and subdivisions were not recorded\. Those that were legally registered usually had defective descriptions and the trees, rocks, and natural landmarks defining the corners were soon disturbed\. Numerous problems in land surveying stem from the confusion of early property titles, descriptions, and poor surveying equipment\. The locations of many corners have been established by compromise after resurveys or by court interpretation of their original or intended positions\.

title: Point of Commencement
text:
A __metes and bounds __description sets forth and completely describes the boundary lines for a particular parcel of land\. It usually begins with an introduction that locates the land in a general part of the state \(e\.g\., the name of the city, county, and state in which it is located\) followed by an established point, the location of which is acknowledged by local surveyors\. This point, usually designated by a monument, is known as the __point of commencement__\. The initial point of commencement is often a section corner\. However, the point of commencement may also be an established point, such as “the intersection of the east line of Smith Road with the south right\-of\-way line of U\.S\. HWY 49\.”

A __monument __is a physical object that marks the location of a survey point or boundary line\. Monuments are classified as either natural or artificial\. __Natural monuments __such as rivers, lakes, oceans, cliffs, trees, hills, and large boulders are permanent objects found on the land as they were placed by nature and are usually considered controlling over __artificial monuments __\(man\-made\) such as iron stakes, wooden stakes, rock mounds, stones, and wooden fences\. Some man\-made monuments, because of the certainty of location, visibility, stability, and permanence, are considered equal in rank to natural monuments\. In this classification would fall sidewalks, street paving, curbs, wells, canals, concrete buildings, and concrete fences\. A good monument should possesses the quality of being easily visible, clearly identifiable, stable in location, permanent in character, and nondependent upon measurement for its location\. An artificial monument possess the qualities of a natural monument to a lesser degree\. Thus a stake placed in the

ground will rust or rot with time and is less permanent than a large boulder\. A stake is easier to move than a boulder and is, therefore, less stable\.

title: Point of Beginning
text: Once the point of commencement is established, the metes and bounds description must then lead to the __point of beginning __of the subject parcel of land\. The point of beginning must be precise or the entire description will be incorrect\. It must be a definitely ascertainable point and a point that can be located on the ground\. Therefore, a point of beginning must be either \(a\) at a known point \(a monument, man\-made or natural\), such as a section corner, street corner, street intersection, etc\., or \(b\) a certain course and distance from a monument\. From the point of beginning, the metes and bounds description then proceeds around the boundary line of the subject parcel of land by directions that usually are expressed in “courses and distances” commonly referred to as calls\.

title: Courses
text:
The __course __is the direction in which the boundary line travels\. A __boundary line __is a line of demarcation between adjoining parcels of property\. A __call __is a reference to, or statement of, an object, course, distance or other matter of description in a survey\.

The course of a boundary line is usually done by course bearings\. A __bearing __\(also known as a course bearing\) is the direction of a line measured as the angle from a reference point\. Bearings are based on true north or true south compass readings, and each course is based on a north\-south direction\. The compass directions are based on a 360\-degree radius, for which there are four 90\-degree quadrants: northwest, northeast, southeast, and southwest\.

title: Courses
text: Each quadrant has 90 __degrees__\. Each degree has 60 __minutes__\. Each minute has 60 __seconds__\. Degrees, minutes, and seconds are often abbreviated using the °, ′, ″ symbols respectively\. Thus, an angle described as 35° 30′ 42″ means 35 degrees 30 minutes 42 seconds\. This angle is then more than 35 degrees, but less than 36 degrees\. For purposes of sketching a legal description, it is acceptable to round off the minutes and seconds of an angle\. Thus, 35° 30′ 42″ would be treated as 35°\. See diagram below\.

title: Courses
text:
To further illustrate, a line that is north 45 degrees west would be found in the northwest quadrant of the compass \(See P, in the diagram below\)\. A line that is south 45 degrees east would be found in the southeast quadrant of the compass \(See Q, in the diagram below\)\.

![](data:image/png;base64,

title: Courses
text:
Some descriptions contain angles \(rather than bearings\), which represent the angle measured in the field by a surveyor and mapper\. These angles refer back to the previous line rather than to a meridian\.

__Angles __in a legal description indicate the direction of a property line instead of \(or in addition to\) bearings\. As noted earlier, a circle has 360 __degrees__, with each degree having 60 __minutes __and each minute having 60 __seconds__, which forms the basis of angles used in legal descriptions\. Both angles and bearings use of the terms “degrees,” “minutes,” and “seconds;” however, the methods of measurement are different\.

title: Courses
text:
A line running “northeasterly at an interior angle of 60 degrees 14 minutes 30 seconds” differs from a line running “north 60 degrees 14 minutes 30 seconds east\.” An angle runs from the last described course and is either interior \(inside the property boundaries\) or exterior \(outside the property boundaries\)\.

When angles are used to describe courses, the property corners intersect at two lines\. The intersection of those two lines is the center of the circle\. The arc of the circle within the boundary is the interior angle, and the arc outside the property boundary is the exterior angle\. In the example below, there is an interior angle of 85 degrees and an exterior angle of 275 degrees at one corner\. At another corner, there is an interior angle of 270 degrees and an exterior angle of 90 degrees\.

title: Courses
text:
The calls used to describe these angles could be any of the following:

__thence north at an interior angle of 85 degrees \(exterior angle of 275 degrees from the last described course\); thence east at an interior angle of 85 degrees \(exterior angle of 275 degrees from the last described course\); thence south at an interior angle of 270 degrees \(exterior angle 90 degrees\) from the last described course; thence east at an interior angle of 270 degrees \(exterior angle 90 degrees\) from the last described course\.__

When angles are used, the interior and exterior angles are always the same, even though the property lines are described from different locations\. Generally, only one interior or exterior angle is shown

at a corner, not necessarily both\. However, a circle always has 360 degrees, and the omitted angle can easily be computed if necessary\.

title: Curves
text:
It is important to note that not all property can be measured in straight lines\. Sometimes a metes and bounds description involves a curved land boundary\. A __curve __is a part of the arc of a circle\. It is limited at each end by the radii of the circle which form a central angle at the center of the circle\.

Elements of a curve are identified as parts of a sector of a circle\. Below is an example of the elements of a curve used in mapping:

title: Curves
text: ![C:\Users\kfarmer\Box Sync\LTAMS\01 - Graphics Files\17 - Certification Graphics\Metes & Bounds\MB 75.png](data:image/png;base64,

title: Curves
text:
An __arc __is a part of the circumference of a circle or curve\.

A __chord __is a straight line drawn from the beginning point of the arc to the ending point of the arc\.

__Radius __is the distance from a point on the curve to the center of the circle\.

__Arc length __or __length of \(along\) curve __is the linear measurement of the curve\.

__Concavity __is the inside or indented side of the curve\. Conversely, the convex side of a curve is the outside or the side of the curve away from the center of the circle\.

__Direction upon a curve __is the general bearing along the curve \(such as northerly, southerly, southwesterly, etc\.\) Direction applied to concavity specifies the bearing from the concave curve at its midpoint to the center of the circle\.

__Tangency __occurs when a curve is tangent to a course at a point if the radius of the curve at that point makes an angle of 90° with the course\. A __tangent line __is a straight line that touches the circumference of a circle at only one point\. A tangent line is often called the tangent\.

__Radial bearings __are furnished if a curve is not tangent to a course at the point of intersection thereof\.

The length and bearing of the radius must be given to determine the center of the circle\.

Whenever a legal description involves a curve, the following information is generally required in order to plot the description: \(a\) the arc length or length along the curve; \(b\) the radius distance of the curve;

\(c\) the chord course and distance; and \(d\) the direction of the curve\.

title: Curves
text: ![C:\Users\kfarmer\Box Sync\LTAMS\01 - Graphics Files\17 - Certification Graphics\Metes & Bounds\MB 76.png](data:image/png;base64,

title: Curves
text:
An example of a curved metes and bounds description might read as follows:

__Beginning at point North 0°13’ East 195\.63 feet along the section line from the Southwest corner of Section 15, Township 5 North, Range 1 West, Some County, Mississippi\. Running thence North 0°13’ East 362\.81 feet; thence North 75°56’26” East__

__140\.33 feet; thence to the left 260 feet along the arc of a curve whose radius is 356\.37 feet whose chord bears South 34°57’37” East 254\.22 feet; thence South 29°18’36” West__

__43\.50 feet; thence to the right 317\.16 feet along the arc of a curve whose radius is__

__295\.05 feet and whose chord bears South 60°06’18” West 302\.11 feet to the point of beginning\.__

title: Curves
text: On some occasions a property description will not contain a chord, in this event it must be assumed, when totally void of all other information, that the curve is a regular curve with the radius being at a right angle \(90°\) to the last course given, and that it is tangent to the bearing of the previous line\.

title: Distance
text:
A legal description must set forth the distance of each property line or provide information to determine the distance so that the property lines and corners can be ascertained\. The sole purpose of distance in connection with the validity of a legal description is as a means of locating the corners\.

__Distance __in a legal description indicates the length of the property line\. Most recent instruments set forth distances in feet and hundredths of a foot\. A call that is 56\.8 feet is 56 and 80/100ths of a foot in length\.

At each corner of the parcel being described, a new course and distance are given\. A simple and complete metes and bounds description might read as follows:

__Commence at the Northwest corner of Section 7, Township 3 South, Range 25 East; thence run Southerly along the West line of said section 965 feet to the point of beginning; thence continue along said line 100 feet; thence run South 89° 30′ 30″ East 150 feet; thence run Northerly and parallel with the West line of said section 100 feet, thence run North 89° 30′ 30″ West 150 feet, more or less, to the point of beginning\.__

In the example above, the course of the first call of the parcel of land is southeast\. The distance of the call is 150 feet\. The bearing for the west line of the section has been omitted in the above description\. A statement of the bearing of a section line is not essential\. However, this description would be more complete and informative if it was included\.

It is important to note that the instruments and tools used to measure the land by surveyors during the early and late 1800s and early 1900s were crude by today’s standards\. The distance was recorded utilizing the common unit of measurement for that period which was based on the chain\. The chain measurement is a geodetic system, formerly popular in Britain and its colonies\. It was developed in the 17th century by Edmund Gunter and is rarely used today in the United States\.

Gunter used an actual measuring chain of 100 __links__\. These, the chain and the link, have become units of their own\. A __chain __is 4 rods long, with the __rod __being a standardized measurement of 5 ½ yards or 16 ½ feet\. This rod is also called a perch or a pole\. A chain is 22 yards or 66 feet in length\. A __link __is 1 chain divided by 100; or exactly 7\.92 inches \(or 0\.66 feet\) in length\.

title: Introduction
text: Well\-drafted metes and bounds descriptions may be read like a story and are generally divided into four parts: a caption \(the preamble\), a heading \(the beginning\), a body \(the plot thickens\), and one or more closing clauses \(an end\)\. Although in writing a particular description the four parts may be intermingled to make it difficult to distinguish one part from another, it is a better practice, when feasible, to keep the four parts distinctly separated\.

title: Caption
text:
The __caption __serves as an introduction to the description and contains a general location reference to indicate to the reader where the lands are located\. It may site the section, township, range, city \(optional\), county \(optional\), state \(optional\) or meridian \(required only if the previous items are left out\) or some other such indicator like a subdivision’s name and recording information\. It may also contain a parent tract citation, being a recital of the book and page in the public records of the tract from which the new parcel is partitioned\. The caption serves as a legal limit to the lands conveyed such that if the body of the description included lands located outside of those captioned, only the captioned land is transferred\. It usually ends with the words “\.\.\.more particularly described as follows:\.\.\.” or “\.\.\.being more specifically described as follows:\.\.\.”\.

The wording of the caption may take many forms, but here is one example:

__A parcel of land being situated in the Northwest 1/4 of Section 23, Township 11 North, Range 3 East, Madison County, Mississippi, and being more particularly described by metes and bounds as follows: \.\.\.__

The details of the location of the lands being described are contained within the heading and body of the description\.

title: Heading
text:
The __heading__, if any, contains the calls necessary to get one from the point where the description starts to the point of beginning\. It is not required as the description may begin at a point on the perimeter \(boundary line\) of the lands being described\. It is started with a point of commencement which is used to reference the parcel to some well\-established point\. Such a point may typically include a government survey corner, a long established artificial monument or the intersecting points of two streets, whatever the author felt was unmistakable, then the calls necessary to get the reader “to the point of beginning”\. If it is present,

it will usually end with the words “\.\.\.to the Point of Beginning:\.\.\.” and if it is not, than it will usually start with the words “Commence at …,” “Begin at \.\.\.,” “Commencing at …,” or “Beginning at\.\.\.”\.

__Commence at a found CPS marking the Northeast corner of the Southeast 1/4 of Section 22 per that deed recorded in Book 501 at Page 001 \(reference to said deed being made as a part of this description\); run thence East for a distance of 27\.18 feet to a point on the Eastern Right\-of\-Way line of Old Highway 51 and the POINT OF BEGINNING for the parcel herein described; …__

Remember, in a metes and bounds description, a point of commencement is not always necessary, but a point of beginning is required\.

title: Body
text:
The __body __of a description identifies a particular land area within the locality designated by the caption\. The body of the description is made up of the number of changes of direction \(calls\) necessary to __traverse __\(move along the course of a legal description or trace a property boundary\) around the subject parcel\. The sequence of the described courses traversing the parcel follows the point of beginning in the same paragraph, with the last course returning “to the point of beginning”\.

__from said point of beginning, run along said Right\-of\-Way North 02 degrees 33 minutes 43 seconds East for a distance of 417\.28 feet; thence run 387\.57 feet along the arc of a 1574\.39 foot radius curve to the right, said arc having a 386\.59 foot chord bearing North 06 degrees 19 minutes 19 seconds East; thence North 12 degrees 17 minutes 42 seconds East for a distance of 12\.17 feet; thence leave said Right\-of\-Way and run South 89 degrees 54 minutes 53 seconds East for a distance of 255\-0\. 73 feet; thence South 00 degrees 05 minutes 07 seconds West for a distance of809\.19 feet; thence West for a distance of 2613\.33 feet to the point of beginning\.__

The body, taken together with the caption and heading \(if any\), must identify a certain area; otherwise, the conveyance will be void\. The body should contain complete dimensional information that renders the intent of the deed certain and clear\.

The body is a combination of all or portions of the following elements used to describe the land and to reference its location to the surrounding lands:

- Point of beginning
- Courses \(bearing or direction\)
- Distance
- Calls by reference
- Calls for monuments and bounds or adjoining lands with qualifying terms and descriptions
- Closing call to the point of beginning or other known locatable point or line
- Area of land contained \(if applicable\)
- Basis of bearings
- Any additional information that can assist with the accurate location of the land being described \(such as clauses\)

Abbreviations should be avoided whenever possible\. However, certain words are commonly abbreviated\. The following is a list of common abbreviations used in metes and bounds descriptions:

It should be noted that a description must close to be valid\. In other words, the description must commence at the point of beginning, follow each course and distance, and end at the exact point of beginning\. Closure problems can be created by erroneous points of beginning, erroneous courses, and erroneous distances\.

title: Closing Clauses
text:
After one is returned to the point of beginning, sometimes the author may feel that various statements are necessary to make the reader more knowledgeable of the author’s intent of the extent of the lands included or of the control items under which the description was prepared\. Words or phrases like the size of the parcel involved, the method of treating the beginning and starting “cutoff” lines if a strip description, the bearing basis, etc\.

Closing clauses are usually at the end of the body of a land description and are for the purpose of clarifying, encumbering, taking away from, adding to, or restricting something with reference to the land being described\. Closing clauses may also include statements of content \(acreage or square footage\), exceptions, easements, and other restrictions upon use of the property\. For example:

__This parcel contains 48\.29 acres \(2,103,358\.93 square feet\), more or less\.__

__*Augmenting clauses *__describe any additional title rights or interests and appurtenances that are not included in the body of the description, such as an easement for ingress and egress\. These clauses are normally preceded by the words “together with” or “and including\.”

Here are some augmenting clause examples:

__AND TOGETHER WITH: A 30\-foot ingress/egress easement being situated in the Northwest 1/4 of Section 23, Township 11 North, Range 3 East, Madison County, Mississippi, and being more particularly described by metes and bounds as follows:__

__\.\.\.__

__*Qualifying clauses *__exclude, modify or encumber described land, such as the reservation of land for roadway purposes or exception of lands, easements and other restrictions\. These clauses are normally preceded by the words “subject to,” “reserving,” or “less and except\.” __*Subject to *__refers to a reservation already existing; when used in a conveyance, it means “subordinate to,” “subservient to,” “limited by,” or “charged to\.” __*Reserving *__means keeping a certain right from the area just granted or taking back a part of something granted\. __*Less and except *__or __*excepting *__means excluding from the area or cutting off a portion of the whole area that has just been described, or withdrawals from the description of the property conveyed\. When exception and reservation are used together, the customary meaning holds that certain property is withdrawn from the description of what is conveyed and an independent right to an interest in the land is created and vested in the grantor\. In the context of split estates, a provision excepting and reserving the mineral estate retains and creates title to the mineral estate in the grantor\.

Here are some qualifying clause examples:

__LESS AND EXCEPT: A parcel of land being situated in the Northwest 1/4 of Section 23, Township 11 North, Range 3 East, Madison County, Mississippi, and being more particularly described by metes and bounds as follows: \.\.\.__

__*Controlling clauses *__describe terms of expressed or special intent, such as a record survey, deed conveyance referral, basis for bearings and directions, and any other conditions controlling the described parcel\. For example, when a land description has been updated by a survey:

__And being the same property described in Warranty Deed recorded in Book 2019, at Page 529\.__

__\-\- or \-\-__

__A Certificate of Survey Plat prepared by \[Surveyor Name\], dated \[date\], is attached hereto and made a part hereof\.__

External evidence may prove that the terms were not used according to their usual and different connotations\.

Descriptions may be divided into two or more parts or parcels for convenience in form or for segregation with respect to other considerations in the document\. Usually, a well\-written description will separate fee and easement parcels, for example\.

title: Point of Beginning
text: It is not unusual to find the point of commencement of a metes and bounds description referred to as the first or initial “point of beginning” of the description, and the actual point of beginning of the parcel also referred to as the “point of beginning\.” It is confusing and incorrect to refer to the point of commencement in this fashion\. The point of commencement must be established by reference to a monument or a reference that is correctly tied to such a marker\.

title: Closure
text: Every metes and bounds description should return to the point of beginning and it is appropriate that the description close with this reference point\. This is a critical aspect of establishing the accuracy of the metes and bounds description\. If the description does not close by having the various courses and distances intersect at the identical point of beginning, the description is void\. Generally, reference to the final call as running to the point of beginning is made, but this does not ensure closure\. A survey is essential and is the only reliable verification of the accuracy of the description\. In the absence of a survey, the courses and distances can be plotted on a blank section map to facilitate the examination of an abstract or title search, but this should not be used as a substitute for the boundary survey\.

title: Reversed or Erroneous Bearings
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-243 - Reversed or Erroneous Bearings
text: Another commonly overlooked error in metes and bounds descriptions is a reversed or erroneous bearing\. A drafter of descriptions sometimes may insert a “north” where a “south” is appropriate\. Errors are also made in the call of an angle or distance such as a call bearing along a section or fractional section line\. The result may be a deviation of a few degrees on the wrong side of true north, south, east, or west\. It also could result in a bearing that is 180 degrees in the wrong direction\. Because this occurs frequently, all title examinations should be conducted with care and attention to detail\.

title: Curve Data
text: Curves that are a part of a metes and bounds description are difficult to validate unless the title examiner is proficient in geometry\. This is one of the exclusive responsibilities of the surveyor\. The examining attorney should verify that the curve data in a description were prepared by a surveyor\.

title: Gaps and Overlaps
text: Gaps and overlaps may occur in metes and bounds descriptions\. These are not apparent from a record examination but will be ascertained when the property is surveyed\. If a description commences from a point in another section, or the description has been prepared on the assumption that the section, including the subject property, is regular in size and oriented to true north, there is a likelihood that a gap or overlap will occur\. The boundary survey will reveal if this has occurred and will guide future description preparation to avoid this type of error\.

title: Omitted or Erroneous Calls
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-246 - Omitted or Erroneous Calls
text:
A metes and bounds description with numerous calls is more likely to include a call or angle that is incorrect or even omitted\. This is not to say that an omission will not occur with a short description, but there is a greater chance for omission when the description is long and complex\. In many circumstances, the

omission is apparent and is discovered if the examining attorney plots out the description at the time the title is evaluated\.

To avoid errors such as omitted calls, the attorney should prepare the legal description as a separate file document or as a schedule for attachment\. The description must be proofread for accuracy and then saved to the computer files in both word processing and pdf formats to be inserted or appended to the transaction documents as needed\. This will save the extra effort of retyping a metes and bounds description numerous times, and will reduce the risk of error\. The text of the transaction documents should incorporate by reference any schedule containing a description\.

title: Conflict with Acreage Reference
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-247 - Conflict with Acreage Reference
text:
If a conflict exists between the stated acreage of a tract and the acreage computed from a metes and bounds description, a “red flag” is raised alerting the attorney that further examination is needed\. The attorney should carefully compare the survey with the legal description\.

When used in connection with quantity or distance in a conveyance of land, the words __more or less __are considered words of safety or precaution, intended to cover some slight or unimportant inaccuracy\. The same applies to the use of the word “about\.”

title: General Rule
text:
When the lines of an old survey are being relocated, or a discrepancy exists between two tracts, the following precedence \(weight of importance\) usually applies:

1. The lines actually run on the ground by the creating surveyor\(s\)\. This includes corners established, monuments set, and lines marked on the ground at the time of creating a survey\.
2. Calls for monuments set at the time of the survey or that enjoy a clear chain of history back to the original monuments:
	1. Natural monuments set at the time of the original survey\.
	2. Artificial monuments set and referred to in the description\.
3. Calls for adjoining parcels that are senior in title and called for and identified in the survey and called for in the description\.
4. Calls for courses \(bearings\)\.
5. Calls for distances\.
6. Calls for area or acreage\.

title: Applying Priority of Calls
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-250 - Applying Priority of Calls
text:
All lines marked and surveyed, when positively identified, identify the true intended boundaries of the parcel and as such will control over less certain elements in the description\. These lines constitute the true intended boundaries and will yield to less certain elements\. This element is generally not considered by title examiners\. If a field survey were conducted and monuments were set, if the surveyor had the notes identifying the corners, and if the surveyor went on the ground and found them, then the original survey controls\. If no lines were called for or if the surveyor went on to the ground and found nothing but called for

monuments identified in the notes, both natural or artificial, these control over the marked lines\. Thus, examiners generally start with the next category – monuments set\.

Calls for natural or permanent objects or monuments, definitely located, will generally control over other and conflicting calls unless a different intent is determined\. These are the next elements in the order of control only if they can be located on the ground\. This rule is flexible and open to construction in that it must be proven that the natural monument was intended\. If natural monuments are not called for or cannot be identified, then one may rely on artificial monuments called for, if it can be determined that the artificial monument is the more certain of the two\.

An adjoining parcel may be considered as a natural boundary in the light that natural or artificial monuments are neither called for nor unascertainable\. If the adjoining line is senior in time, well defined, and called for as an established line, one may accept the calls for the adjoining line\. One must be careful to make certain that the line called for is senior and is the line and not its extension\.

If no lines are run or found, no monuments set or called for or found, and no adjoining parcels called for or identified in the description, then one may resort to courses \(bearings\) and distances\. Bearings control over distances\. If courses must be used, then each line must be analyzed independently and in conjunction with all other lines\.

Area or “acreage” is the least controlling of all the elements\. Area, or quantity of acreage, depends

on calculations and adjustments\. Since property is rarely square, there is no absolute area ascertainment\.

title: Land measure compass
text:
The land measure compass is a specific type of protractor for measuring or laying out of angles or based on compass direction usually referred to as bearings\. The Land Measure Compass is laid out in a full circle and is broken into four 90° directional quadrants with the measurements divided into degrees and half\-degrees\. It has a movable arm for assistance measuring existing angles\.

![](data:image/png;base64,

title: Land measure compass
text:
Within a metes and bounds description, the bearings and distances of each traverse are listed\. A bearing is defined as “direction of a line measured as the angle from a reference meridian”\. Therefore, in a metes and bounds description, a typical traverse could look something like: North 45° West, for 595’\. Using the land measure compass, starting at North 0°, move 45° counter\-clockwise, which is West\. This would be

the bearing\. The distance from Point A to Point B in this example is 595’\. A traverse includes a bearing and a distance\.

title: Drafting triangle
text:
The drafting triangle is a typical right angle triangle except that it includes helpful information\. Right triangles are needed to keep parcel drawings square, as well as identifying right angles when calculating the area of a right triangle\.

![](data:image/png;base64,

title: Drafting scale
text:
Drawings are made to a certain scale\. __Scale __represents the ratio or relationship between the distance on a survey map or plat and the actual distance on the ground that is represented by the map or plat\. Usually the drawing is a reduced scale but in some cases, it is enlarged beyond actual size in order to show details\. One unit of measurement on the map – 1 inch or 1 centimeter – could represent 10,000 of the same units on the ground\. This would be a 1:10,000 scaled map\.

Scales are classified as either metric or English\. The English is divided into architectural, engineering, and mechanical groups\. The most commonly used scale in the construction, maintenance and reading of survey maps and plats is the engineer’s twelve\-inch long triangular scale\. It is divided decimally into ten units per inch, 20 units per inch, 30 units per inch, 40 units per inch, 50 units per inch and 60 units per inch\. These are commonly referred to as 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 or 60 scales\.

Depending on the size of the parcel and the size of the paper, different scales can be used\. For example, if a parcel is to be drawn on a sheet of paper that is 8 ½ x 11, and the longest line of the parcel is 1,320’, a scale of 1” =100’ could not be used because that would result in the longest line being 13\.2” long\. Therefore, it is important to review the legal description and determine the size of the map before selecting the scale at which the map will be drawn\.

title: Drafting scale
text: To use any scale, lay the scale on a surface parallel to a line\. Use a sharp pencil to mark all measurements before moving the scale\. Your moving the scale for each measurement increases the likelihood of a cumulative error\. Indicate the measurements with a sharp pencil\. Do not draw against the machined increment of the scale, instead use a straight edge to draw you line\.

title: How to Convert Map Scale
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-256 - How to Convert Map Scale
text:
As described above, it is important to understand map scale\. In order to convert property line distances into map scale to represent the line appropriately on the map, divide the legal description measurement by the map scale\.

For instance, if the paper to map scale 1” = 100’, then 1 inch on the map equals 100 feet on the

ground\.

__Example__:	North 45° West, for 595’ with a map with a scale of 1” = 100’ 595’ ÷ 100’ = 5\.95”

This means that your 595 feet long line on a map with a map scale of 1” = 100’, will equal a line 5\.95

inches long\.

This method is also necessary when the map scale is different than the map scale of your legal description\. For example, historic maps were drawn at a scale of 1” = 660’\. The only way to draw legal description measurements on a map is with a ruler\. So, using the conversion method above:

595’ \(feet\) ÷ 660’ \(feet\) = \.90” \(inches\)

title: How to Read and Draw Compass Bearings
parent_hierarchy: How to Read and Draw Compass Bearings
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-257 - How to Read and Draw Compass Bearings
text: Line your compass up on the following diagram\. The north and south arrows should indicate 0°\. The east and west arrows should indicate 90°\. If a legal description calls for a line North 45° West, you would first start with the North 0° point on your compass, then move along the compass to the West \(your left\), until you reach 45°\. Your bearing would be the line of the arrow marked NW\. If a legal description calls for a line South 45° East, you would first start with the South 0° point on your compass\. Then, move along the compass to the east \(your right\) until you reach 45°\. Your point would be the line of the arrow marked SE\.

text:
__Step 5__:

Place the land measure compass on top of Point A, ready for the next measurement in the legal description\.

At this point, it is important to be sure that the land measure compass is oriented on the page the same way as it was when beginning the drawing\.

Otherwise, even a small twist in the compass could have dramatic effects\.

To avoid this problem, “backsighting” is used\. A backsight is defined as “reading taken by a surveyor back toward a position from which a previous sight has been made\.” On the land measure compass, the backsight is the opposite of the bearing previously used\.

Since the previous bearing was N 80° E, the backsight is S 80° W\. So, orienting the land measure compass on the map with the center over Point A, and the line drawn matching up with S 80° W indicates that the compass is now sitting on the page the same way as when the drawing began\.

Without moving the land measure compass, make a mark on the map using the second bearing \(S 45° E\)\. This time look at due South\. Make the mark that

is 45° East \(counterclockwise\) of South\.

__*NOTE*__*: The ruler in the above example says “100 FT to the Inch” \(this is the same as the “10 Scale” on the triangular ruler\. However, the images in the example are NOT to scale \(meaning you can’t print this out and line up the ruler with the image\)\.*

__Step 3__:

Remove the land measure compass, and using a drafting scale, place the “0” on the POB, and line up the scale with the mark made at the N 80° E bearing\. Then draw a line that represents 350’\. With a map scale of 1” = 100’, that would be a line that is

3\.5” long \(to Point A\)\. The mark you made at N 80° E only gives the direction \(bearing\) of the line\. The drafting scale shows the length of the line\.

__Step 4:__

It is recommended that each line be labeled with both bearings and distances \(traverse\) as it is drawn, so that if a problem is discovered, the information from the legal description is right there on the drawing\. Therefore, above the line you just drew, write out N 80° E 350’\.

__Step 10__:

Place the land measure compass on top of Point C\. Backsight the previous line to be sure the compass is oriented correctly\.

The previous bearing was S 60° W\. Therefore, the backsight is N 60° E\. Turn the land measure compass until the last line drawn lines up with N 60° E\.

__*NOTE*__*: The ruler in the above example says “100 FT to the Inch” \(this is the same as the “10 Scale” on the triangular ruler\. However, the images in the example are NOT to scale \(meaning you can’t print this out and line up the ruler with the image\)\.*

__Step 3__:

Remove the land measure compass, and using a drafting scale, place the “0” on the POB, and line up the scale with the mark made at the N 80° E bearing\. Then draw a line that represents 350’\. With a map scale of 1” = 100’, that would be a line that is

3\.5” long \(to Point A\)\. The mark you made at N 80° E only gives the direction \(bearing\) of the line\. The drafting scale shows the length of the line\.

__Step 4:__

It is recommended that each line be labeled with both bearings and distances \(traverse\) as it is drawn, so that if a problem is discovered, the information from the legal description is right there on the drawing\. Therefore, above the line you just drew, write out N 80° E 350’\.

title: Overview
parent_hierarchy: CHAPTER 20: LOT AND BLOCK SURVEY SYSTEM
text: This chapter covers the lot and block survey system \(also known as the subdivision system, the recorded plat survey system, or the recorded map survey system\)\. The purpose of this chapter is to provide a detailed understanding of how a subdivision plat is created, the component parts of a subdivision plat, and how to locate real property using the lot and block survey system\.

- Understand the component parts of a subdivision plat
- Identify and locate a lot and block parcel on a subdivision plat

title: Background
parent_hierarchy: CHAPTER 20: LOT AND BLOCK SURVEY SYSTEM
text:
During the early settlement of what is now known as the United States, real property was conveyed with lengthy legal descriptions using physical features of the local geography \(trees, rivers, rocks\), along with directions and distances measured with tools known as links, chains, and rods\. This system and the

tools used varied from place to place and there was minimal consistency\. The Public Land Survey System \(PLSS\) was developed in the early 1800s to establish a uniform grid system of sections, townships, and ranges\. The PLSS forms the foundation for the legal descriptions that we utilize today\.

By the turn of the twentieth century, the demand for smaller pieces of property increased as areas began to urbanize\. Using the PLSS as a base, the lot and block survey system evolved as an efficient way to allow cities and towns to expand into the surrounding rural areas\. Property owners would subdivide their large properties into smaller blocks and lots, file the resulting “subdivision plat” with the official government record keeper, and then sell these pieces of property to buyers\. However, the uncontrolled subdivision of land resulted in inadequate streets, sewers and water mains, and in the extension of public services far beyond their usable capacity\. Urban areas began to suffer from disorderly, chaotic growth and depressed land values\.

In an effort to combat the effects of subdivision, state and local governments began to enact various forms of subdivision regulations\. These early efforts, however, were not designed to eliminate the problems of speculation and sprawl\. The primary purpose of early subdivision regulations was to provide a more efficient method for selling land by permitting a seller to record a subdivision plat which divided a large parcel of land into sequentially numbered blocks and lots\. Sales of the land were then recorded in the office of the county clerk or recorder of deeds by reference to the blocks and lots\.

In 1928, a new form of subdivision regulation was introduced with the publication of the [Standard](https://planning-org-uploaded-media.s3.amazonaws.com/legacy_resources/growingsmart/pdf/CPEnabling%20Act1928.pdf) [City Planning Enabling Act](https://planning-org-uploaded-media.s3.amazonaws.com/legacy_resources/growingsmart/pdf/CPEnabling%20Act1928.pdf) \(“SPEA”\) by the United States Department of Commerce\. The SPEA offered a partial response to the problems created by land speculation and premature subdivision\. It required internal improvements to be made in the subdivision, and addressed issues such as the arrangement of streets in relation to other existing or planned streets and to the master plan; the provision of adequate and convenient open spaces, utilities, access of firefighting apparatus, recreation, light and air; and the avoidance of population congestion, including minimum width and lot areas\. Many states soon adopted subdivision enabling legislation patterned after the SPEA and subdivision regulations gained acceptance as an important Local land use control measure\.

Following World War II, subdivision regulations entered the third phase with the emphasis shifting to the needs of new subdivision residents for public open space, parks and recreation facilities and adequate streets bordering the subdivision\. Local regulations reflected these needs by the imposition of new requirements for the mandatory dedication of roads, parkland, school sites, and open space\. In spite of these expanded regulations, urban sprawl and its attendant problems continued\. New techniques began to emerge which more closely linked the three principal police power controls of zoning, subdivision, and environmental regulations to assure that new development did not impose unreasonable negative impacts on the community\. In addition, subdivision regulations were expanded to help time and phase the development of the community\.

Recent years have witnessed several important trends in subdivision regulation throughout the United States\. First, subdivision approvals are increasingly being predicated on the availability of adequate public services and facilities concurrent with the impacts of the development\. Second, impact fee payments are being required of developers who create a need for or benefit from the provision of public facilities such as roads, parks, libraries, and water and sewer facilities\. Finally, use decisions are being more closely examined in terms of their consistency with the community's comprehensive plan\.

title: Enabling Legislation
parent_hierarchy: CHAPTER 20: LOT AND BLOCK SURVEY SYSTEM
text:
It wasn’t until 1950 that Mississippi adopted subdivision regulation enabling statutes\. See Miss\. Code Ann\. §§ 17\-1\-1 et seq\. These enabling statutes do not define subdivision or even contain a penalty clause\. Instead, they simply empower local governing boards, including municipalities, to adopt and enforce zoning and subdivision regulations\. See Miss\. Code Ann\. § 17\-1\-23\(2\) \(county board of supervisors\); Miss\. Code

Ann\. § 17\-1\-23\(3\) \(municipalities\)\. For a local governing boards subdivision regulations to be enforceable, the statutory requirements and procedures enumerated by Miss\. Code Ann\. §§ 17\-1\-1 et seq\. must be complied with\.

For purposes of this chapter, __subdivision regulation __refers to a subdivision ordinance adopted by a local governing body that regulates the division of privately owned real property into smaller parcels to ensure that there are adequate facilities such as parks, streets, utilities, drainage, and other infrastructure to handle the development of the lots created by the subdivision\. The word __subdivision __\(to subdivide, subdividing\) refers to the division of land without regard to the transfer of ownership\. Subdividing is not the same as platting\. __Platting __\(to plat\) refers to the process required by the government to obtain approval of a subdivision\.

title: Subdivision Plat
parent_hierarchy: CHAPTER 20: LOT AND BLOCK SURVEY SYSTEM
text: A __subdivision plat __\(or plat\) is a map or drawing, prepared in accordance with local subdivision regulations, showing the divisions of a tract of land and the layout of a proposed subdivision including roads and lots at approximate distances and bearings, key plan, topography and drainage, and all proposed facilities at a suitable scale and in such detail as local subdivision regulation may require and containing any information required by the planning board\. Plat review may vary in complexity with regard to the size, location and potential environmental impact of the proposed subdivision\. For example, if a landowner owns two acres of land and wants to divide it into four tracts, a surveyor would have to take precise measurements of the land and submit the survey to the governing body, which would then have to approve it\.

title: Consolidation Plat
parent_hierarchy: CHAPTER 20: LOT AND BLOCK SURVEY SYSTEM
text: A __consolidation plat __originates when a landowner takes over several adjacent parcels of land and consolidates them into a single parcel\. In order to do this, the landowner will usually need to make a survey of the parcels and submit the survey to the governing body that would have to approve the consolidation\.

title: Correction Plat
parent_hierarchy: CHAPTER 20: LOT AND BLOCK SURVEY SYSTEM
text: A __correction plat __makes minor corrections to an existing plat, such as correcting a surveying mistake or a scrivener’s error\. Such plats can sometimes serve to relocate lot\-lines or other features\. Any scrivener’s error which would require the alteration of a lot line must follow the procedures set forth in Miss\. Code Ann\. § 17\-1\-23 or in the alternative, Miss\. Code Ann\. § 19\-27\-31\.

title: Plat Amendment or Replat
parent_hierarchy: CHAPTER 20: LOT AND BLOCK SURVEY SYSTEM
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-303 - Plat Amendment or Replat
text:
A __plat amendment __or a __replat __is a change in a previously recorded subdivision plat that affects the street layout, easements, area reserved for public use, or any lot line\. The only difference between a plat amendment and a replat is the degree to which the plat is amended\. The process for consideration is generally the same as that for the original subdivision plat\.

A plat amendment is necessary when the external boundary of the subdivisions is changed or when a portion which is to be subdivided is to be given a separate lot number\. Miss\. Code Ann\. § 19\-27\-31\. An amendment is not necessary when only a portion of a lot is conveyed by deed to another\. MS AG Op\., Lacoste \(May 1991\)\. In other words, one may convey a portion of a lot without giving the conveyed portion a separate lot number and without having the conveyance marked off on the subdivision plat\.

Miss\. Code Ann\. § 17\-1\-23\(4\) requires that all affected parties be made aware of, and must agree in writing to, the alteration of a subdivision plat\. If an owner obtains the written agreement of all affected parties, then he may petition the board of supervisors for a change in the subdivision plat\. Miss\. Code Ann\. § 17\-1\-

23\(4\)\. If an owner cannot obtain the written agreement of all affected parties, then the board of supervisors or governing authority may not alter the map or plat\. Id\. Instead, the owner must petition the chancery court pursuant to Miss\. Code Ann\. § 19\-27\-31 for a change in the subdivision plat\. Miss\. Code Ann\. 17\-1\-23 provides no definition of “adversely affected” and no definition of “directly interested\.” The determination of those persons that must be named in the petition presented to the board of supervisors and who must agree in writing to the alteration is a question of fact that must be made by the board of supervisors\.

The Chancery Clerk is required to confirm that the local governing body has granted the petition for the alteration of a subdivision plat\. This may be accomplished by the local governing body providing a copy of the resolution or minutes approving the vacating or alteration of the plat or map, since local governing bodies speak only through their minutes\. See Nichols v\. Patterson, 678 So\.2d 673 \(Miss\. 1998\); Thompson

v\. Jones County Community Hospital, 352 So\.2d 795 \(Miss\. 1977\)\. Provided that the local governing body has provided a copy of its minutes or resolution reflecting its approval of the alteration or vacation of the plat or map, the Chancery Clerk has no authority to inquire behind the minutes\.

title: Plat Vacation
parent_hierarchy: CHAPTER 20: LOT AND BLOCK SURVEY SYSTEM
text: A __plat vacation __is a process to legally void all or a portion of a recorded subdivision\. Miss\. Code Ann\. § 17\-1\-23\(4\) requires that all affected parties be made aware of, and must agree in writing to, the vacation of a subdivision plat\. If an owner obtains the written agreement of all affected parties, then he may petition the board of supervisors to vacate a subdivision plat\. Miss\. Code Ann\. § 17\-1\-23\(4\)\. If an owner cannot obtain the written agreement of all affected parties, then the local governing body may not vacate the subdivision plat\. Id\. Instead, the owner must petition the chancery court pursuant to Miss\. Code Ann\. § 19\-27\-31 to vacate the subdivision plat\. Miss\. Code Ann\. 17\-1\-23 provides no definition of “adversely affected” and no definition of “directly interested\.” The determination of those persons that must be named in the petition presented to the board of supervisors and who must agree in writing to the vacation is a question of fact that must be made by the board of supervisors\. A petition for plat vacation may include a request to vacate any recorded covenants that are part of the plat\. The rules normally allow such plats only when all the platted lots remain unsold and no construction of buildings or public improvements has taken place\.

title: Subdivision Procedural Requirements
parent_hierarchy: CHAPTER 20: LOT AND BLOCK SURVEY SYSTEM
text: The process of obtaining approval for a subdivision plat involves the satisfaction of both procedural and substantive requirements\. Most subdivision regulations formally establish a two\-step review and approval process for subdivision plats\. The first step is a review of a preliminary plat, followed by approval of a final plat\. In reality, most local governing boards, whether formally adopted as part of their subdivision regulations or informally practiced, use a four\-step review process:

title: Pre\-Application Meetings
parent_hierarchy: CHAPTER 20: LOT AND BLOCK SURVEY SYSTEM
text:
A __pre\-application meeting __is a meeting between a prospective applicant and local governing body staff to review the prospective application before it is actually filed\. While not every local governing board formally adopts a pre\-application meeting as a required step in the subdivision review process, in reality, most developers will attempt to have one or a series of meetings with the county or municipal staff in order to identify potential issues before going to the expense of preparing a preliminary plat\. Properly organized, the pre\-application meetings can benefit both the applicant and the local governing board, and can save the planning commission many hours of meeting time\.

The subdivision regulations should be viewed as a mechanism for implementing the goals and objectives of the comprehensive plan and as the principal guide for the development of a community\. The applicant should discuss with local governing body staff the policies in the comprehensive plan \(including

the official map\) and the zoning restrictions which may affect the subdivision of the property\. Among the items which should be addressed at the pre\-application stage are the following:

- 
	- 
		- 
			- __Public Use Sites __– Are any future school, park, or other public use sites shown on the comprehensive plan that would involve the property? If so, will the land be acquired? Will some or all of the property be dedicated to the municipality by the developer?
			- __Transportation __– Will major right\-of\-way dedications be required as part of the subdivision? Will a proposed cul\-de\-sac need to be made a through street? Will there be access limitations imposed due to the site’s frontage on a major thoroughfare?
			- __Environment __– Is the property in the flood plain or are there any known wetland areas? As a result of Mississippi’s Endangered Species Protection Act, are there any animals in the vicinity that may use the property as a habitat? Are there any structures or sites on the property that are historic?
			- __Engineering and Utilities __– Are there general or localized engineering issues which need to be addressed as part of the subdivision, e\.g\. drainage, general soil suitability, and so forth?
			- __Zoning Issues __– Will any types of rezoning or variance requests need to accompany the subdivision application?
			- __Procedural Matters __– Does the applicant understand what steps will be involved in the subdivision process and how long approval might take? \(This is the all\-time, number one question of applicants\.\) Does the applicant understand the responsibilities involved, e\.g\., the type of information that must be presented to the planning commission, the number of prints required, and so on? Are there any dedications, exaction or impact fees, or other types of fees or payments that are likely to be required as part of the approval process?

Having these questions addressed early in the process can identify and resolve many issues which otherwise would take up an inordinate amount of the planning commission’s time during the review of the preliminary plat\.

title: Preliminary Plat Review
parent_hierarchy: CHAPTER 20: LOT AND BLOCK SURVEY SYSTEM
text:
A __preliminary plat __is the initial plat prepared by a land surveyor on behalf of a landowner and submitted for “preliminary” governmental approval as part of the platting process\. The preliminary plat serves as a guideline in the preparation of a final plat as well as in the preparation of surveying, engineering and infrastructure plans to serve the plat\.

The preliminary plat stage is when most major issues related to the subdivision should be resolved\. The planning commission’s review of the preliminary plat should identify and resolve the major design issues associated with the subdivision\. One of the key issues to be addressed during the review of a local governing board’s subdivision regulations is what function is to be served by the preliminary plat\. Is the preliminary plat intended to establish the general planning elements of the subdivision, e\.g\., approximate rights\-of\-way width and location of roads, general configuration of lots, and overall relationship to utilities, or should the plat include detailed information concerning engineering issues that may arise during review of the final engineering drawings, e\.g\., size of water and sewer lines, fire hydrant location, and precise storm drainage design? When the preliminary plat review stage is completed, the applicant should know how many lots will be allowed and what is generally expected with regard to major public improvements\.

The level of information that is required to be submitted during the preliminary plat review process is related to the types of development issues facing a local governing board\. Some local governing board allows an applicant to submit “soft line” designs for street and lot layouts for preliminary plats, but some require additional information such as preliminary storm drainage and traffic reports to make certain critical local issues are addressed prior to the approval of the preliminary plat\.

title: Guarantee of Installation of Public Improvements
parent_hierarchy: CHAPTER 20: LOT AND BLOCK SURVEY SYSTEM
Guarantee of Installation of Public Improvements
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-308 - Guarantee of Installation of Public Improvements
text: Many local governing bodies adopt subdivision regulations that establish specific standards to guarantee the installation of required public improvements\. Issues related to the form and amount of the performance guarantee are best addressed during the review of the final engineering plans\.

title: Final Plat Review
parent_hierarchy: CHAPTER 20: LOT AND BLOCK SURVEY SYSTEM
text: A __final plat __is a subdivision plat satisfying all applicable subdivision regulations\. A duplicate original of the final plat is what gets recorded in the plat book\. Following preliminary review and perhaps an engineering review, the final plat must be reexamined to make certain that any design changes that may have been necessary did not cause problems with the configuration and sizes of lots\. The plat is also reviewed at this point to make certain the language regarding such matters as the dedication of rights\-of\-way, notes regarding setbacks and access limitations, and provision of easements reservation are in the proper legal form\.

title: Requirements as to Form
parent_hierarchy: CHAPTER 20: LOT AND BLOCK SURVEY SYSTEM
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-311 - Requirements as to Form
text:
Miss\. Code Ann\. § 19\-27\-23 sets forth the following minimum requirements regarding the form of subdivision plats:

- Scale of not less than 200 feet to an inch
- Muslin backed paper
- 18″ × 24″ in size
- Full legal description showing section, township, and range with section lines drawn on the plat
- Name of city, town, village, or addition
- Names of all owners
- Name of engineer, surveyor, or other person making the map or plat
- Date subdivision plat made
- Signature of owners \(e\.g\., *Owner’s Certificate*\)
- Proper acknowledgment \(e\.g\., *Owner’s Acknowledgment*\)
- Signature of surveyor \(e\.g\., *Surveyor’s/Engineer’s Certificate*\)
- All lots numbered or lettered progressively
- Cardinal points of the compass shown on the plat
- Correct scale

title: Requirements as to Content
parent_hierarchy: CHAPTER 20: LOT AND BLOCK SURVEY SYSTEM
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-312 - Requirements as to Content
text:
Miss\. Code Ann\. § 19\-27\-25 sets forth the following minimum requirements regarding the contents of subdivision plats:

- Description portion of government survey as intended to be platted; or
- Boundaries must be defined by metes and bounds description; and
- Description of all public grounds, by their boundaries, courses, and extent;
- Description of all streets, and alleys designated by their courses, length, widths, names, or numbers, by writing or figures upon that portion of the subdivision plat intended for those uses;
- Lots must be progressively numbered, or, if in blocks, progressively numbered in each block, and the blocks progressively numbered or lettered; and
- Length and width of lots with the same dimensions may be identified upon one tier thereof, but all gores, triangles, or other lots, either squares or parallelograms, shall have the length of their sides plainly defined by figures\.

The foregoing state law substantive requirements \(as to form and content\) are set forth as requirements for a subdivision plat to be recorded, not to be approved; therefore, a subdivision plat could be approved yet still not satisfy the requirements for recordation\. While local governing bodies may adopt subdivision regulations that increase or add to these minimum standards, they cannot reduce them\.

title: Requirements for Recording
parent_hierarchy: CHAPTER 20: LOT AND BLOCK SURVEY SYSTEM
text:
Miss\. Code Ann\. § 19\-27\-27 sets forth the following requirements for recording a subdivision plat after the same has been approved by the local governing board or municipality:

- Both the original and duplicate must be delivered to the Chancery Clerk for examination;
	- If the duplicate fails to conform to the requirements of Miss\. Code Ann\. 19\-27\-23 and 19\-27\-25, then Chancery Clerk must return it for correction; and
	- If the duplicate conforms, then the Chancery Clerk and the engineer or surveyor that created the subdivision plat must certify they have carefully compared the duplicate with the original map or plat, and that it is an exact duplicate thereof \(e\.g\., *Certificate of Comparison*\)\.
- Once certified for comparison, the Chancery Clerk must then:
	- securely fasten the duplicate original in a book of the proper size for the paper so that it will not be folded;
	- the duplicate must be made a record of subdivision plat; and
	- certify on the duplicate the date when and the book and page where it was recorded \(e\.g\.,

*Certificate of Filing and Recordation*\)\.

title: Title Block
text:
Every subdivision plat should contain a __title block__\. The __title block __is the section of the plat that contains basic information about the subdivision\. At a minimum, this includes the name of the subdivision and a brief description of the location of the property\.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,

title: Title Block
text: )The __subdivision’s name __becomes part of the legal descriptions of the newly platted lots\. For this reason, a subdivision cannot have a name identical to another recorded subdivision in the same county\. When a subdivision plat is part of a larger development, the subdivision name will include a reference to the unit or phase of development such as “Phase 1, Phase 2 or No\. 1, No\. 2” and so forth\. Lots within different phases should also be distinctly numbered as 101, 102, 103, 201, 202, 203, 301, 302, 303, etc\.

title: Title Block
text:
If a subdivision plat is replatted or vacated entirely, the new name will include a modifier to make it clear that the updated plat is different from the original plat\. Sometimes subdivision plats also include a statement that it is the final plat\. This is typically a reference to the local review process, which bifurcates local review into a preliminary plat and a final plat\. Generally, only the final plat gets recorded in the land records\.

The title block also includes a brief description of the location of the property shown on the subdivision plat\. This brief description is usually in the form of indexing instructions that describe the quarter\-quarter section, township, and range of the county and state in which the property is located\.

title: Recording Information
text:
Subdivision plats are generally identified by their record location\. The __record location __refers to the book and page or instrument number where the physical copies of the subdivision plats are recorded in the county’s land records\. Each page of the subdivision plat will have its own book and page or instrument number\.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,

title: Recording Information
text:
Every subdivision plat must contain an owner’s certificate signed by all of the record owners\. The __owner’s certificate __usually includes language that \(a\) acknowledges they are the sole owners of the property, and \(b\) expressly dedicates all streets and other public places shown on the subdivision plat, and

vests the fee of or easement over \(as applicable\) those parcels of land in the municipality \(or county\) for the public for the uses named or intended on the plat\.

title: Recording Information
text:
The signature of each owner shown on the plat or on a separate consent to record must be acknowledged by a notary public\. The acknowledgment may be in the long form with specific language relating to each type of ownership such as an individual or business entity\.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,

title: Recording Information
text: )#### Local Approval Information RKhlXKtgjII4I6EEg8GtygAooooAKKKKAP/2Q==)#### Local Approval Information

title: Recording Information
text: Subdivision plats usually include a list of approvals that memorialize the local governing body’s approval process\. Most modern plats include official stamped or signed statements recognizing \(1\) the local governing body’s approval of the plat; \(2\) any zoning approvals for the subdivision, including land development case and environmental review numbers; and \(3\) public works’ approvals of any dedicated rights\-of\-way or other utility infrastructure\. If the plans do not meet the local standards, the plat may include a notation that the rights\-of\-way are not intended for acceptance as a public road\.

title: Recording Information
text:
Subdivision plats should include a scale for engineers and surveyors to determine how the distances drawn in the map are applied on the ground\. As with other types of maps, the __scale __of a subdivision plat describes the relationship between the distance on the plat and the actual distance on the ground that is represented by the plat\. There are three ways of representing this information:

- Verbal scale
- Graphic scale
- Fractional scale \(representative fraction\)

A __verbal scale __is a statement on a map that indicates, for example, “one inch equals one hundred feet,” or “1 inch = 100’\.” This means that every inch measured on the map equals 100 feet on the ground\. Stating a verbal scale tends to be how most people would refer to a map scale in conversation\. If written on a map, however, a verbal scale will no longer be correct if the original map is reduced or enlarged\. Therefore, when dealing with subdivision plats, verbal scale can only be used if the duplicate original that was recorded is the same size as the original version of the plat\. In the image of the example scale below, __verbal scale __can be read as one inch equals one hundred feet \(e\.g\., 1” = 100’\)\.

title: Recording Information
text: )__Graphic scale __\(also known as linear scale or bar scale\) is used for making distance measurements on a map\. Graphic scales are graduated lines \(or bars\) marked with map distances that are proportional to distances on the Earth\. Several different graphic scales may be given on a plat so that different units of measurement may be applied\. Note that the 0 is often NOT on the left edge but rather a small portion of the scale with finer subdivisions than to the right\.

title: Recording Information
text:
The graphic scale is the most useful scale if the plat will be reproduced and changed in size, because both the plat and the graphic scale will change in the same ratio while the other scales will no longer be valid\. The graphic scale is typically reviewed using a triangular engineer’s scale, which is divided into increments of 10 to 60 divisions per inch\. A simple way to use the scale is to cut a strip of paper and place the paper strip on the plat and make hash marks between two points of a line that needs measurement\. Then, compare those hash marks on the strip of paper to the graphic scale to determine the distance\. It is typically easier not to use the edge of the paper strip as the first hash mark, as it can be difficult to determine where the ruler ends\. If the length is more than one graphic scale long, be sure to consider the position of the zero in adding the lengths measured off\. If a non\-linear length is being measured, measure progressive linear segments along the edge of a sheet of paper and use the graphic scale in the same manner\.

The __fractional scale __\(RF or representative fraction\) is a ratio between a unit of distance on the map to the distance that unit represents in reality \(express in the same units\)\. Three basic rules apply\. First, the numerator of the fraction is always ONE\. Second, both numbers represent the SAME UNIT OF MEASUREMENT\. Third, NO UNIT of measurement is ever given with the representative fraction\. The representative fraction is the best scale if a map is not to be reproduced and changed in size because it does not rely on any particular measurement system \(British, Metric\)\. Whatever unit of measurement is represented by the numerator, the denominator represents the exact same unit of measurement\. Representative fractions are generally written as 1:1,200 or 1/1,200\.

When thinking of map scale, it is best to think of scale as a fraction\. As the number represented by the fraction gets larger, so does the scale\. Conversely, as the denominator of the fraction gets larger, the scale gets smaller\. Thus, a map at a scale of 1:2,400 \(1″ = 200′\) is a smaller scale map than a map at a scale of 1:1,200 \(1″ = 100′\)\. A map at a scale of 1:1,200 \(1″ = 100′\) is a smaller scale map than a map at a scale of 1:600 \(1″ = 50′\)\.

title: North Arrow
text: Subdivision plats should include a prominent __north arrow __on every page\. The primary purpose of the north arrow is for orientation\. It allows the viewer to determine the direction of the map as it relates to due north\. Subdivision plats are generally drawn in a north\-south orientation for ease of navigation \(with the north arrow pointing squarely to the top of the printed page\)\. However, subdivision plats may also be oriented with the north arrow in an offset direction\. The plat may also have a second arrow or designation that demonstrates the difference between true north and magnetic north\.

title: Legend
text:
As with any other map, a subdivision plat should have a __legend __– a key to symbols used on the map\. A subdivision plat’s legend provides a guide to the abbreviations used by the surveyor to designate various markings on the map\. These abbreviations and symbols can differ dramatically between surveyors, even within the same county\.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,

title: Legend
text: )The markers and monument symbols are often used as reference points for determining the boundary of the subdivision\. The legend may also describe what the different line segments mean\. For

title: Legend
text: example, a thick black line may designate the border of the lot, while a thinner, dotted line may designate a setback line\.

title: Plat Notes
Surveyor Notes
Surveyor Notes
text:
As with other types of surveys, a professional land surveyor preparing a final subdivision is required to certify his or her work\.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,

title: Surveyor Notes
text: All subdivision plats include a description of the subdivision’s boundary\. The description is usually a metes and bounds description that starts with a point of beginning and follows the bearings and distances of the boundary listed within the plat\. The boundaries are often drawn with black lines that are thicker than other lines noted on the map, such as easements or individual lot lines\.

title: Area Vicinity Maps
text: Plats sometimes include an informal, not\-to\-scale vicinity map that provides the reader context on the general location of the subdivision within the municipality\. The vicinity maps are reference material and do not subdivide land or convey any property rights\.

title: Excluded Property
text: Sometimes subdivision plats exclude properties that are owned by a different entity or reserved by the developer for their personal use or future development\. This may be done by carving the excluded property out the subdivision plat’s boundary line or by adding a note on the plat that a particular portion of the property is excluded or a reserved tract of land\.

title: Reference to Neighboring Properties
citation: abstractor-training-manual § auto-326 - Reference to Neighboring Properties
text:
A subdivision plat’s boundaries may be further defined by references to adjacent properties\. These references help demonstrate how the plat matches up with the boundaries of neighboring subdivisions or tracts of land and avoid unintended gaps, sometimes referred to as a “hiatus,” between the boundaries of the plat and adjacent properties\.

For example, in the sample plat image on the next page, the eastern boundary of an adjacent phase of the subdivision is noted on the plat together with its recordation information \(e\.g\., Hartford Part 1A, Plat Cabinet E, Slot 31A\)\.

text:
Generally, a __lot __is a tract or parcel of land represented and identified by a number or letter designation on a subdivision plat\. Plats use a lot and block survey system to refer to the subdivided parcels of land within the plat\. After the plat is approved and recorded, the developer may sell off the newly\-created lots individually by reference to their location on the plat map\.

text: )In the sample plat image above, the plat describes the dimensions of the lots \(length and width in feet\) and labels the lots with consecutive numbers placed within a circle \(e\.g\., 79, 80, 81, 82, etc\.\)\.

title: Blocks
text: Generally, a __block __is a piece or parcel of land or group of lots located with a subdivision that is entirely surrounded by public streets, streams, railroads, or parks, or combination thereof\. Depending on the size of the subdivision, the lots may be grouped into blocks\. The lots are progressively numbered within each block \(1, 2, 3…etc\.\), and the blocks are typically lettered alphabetically \(A, B, C…etc\.\)\. If blocks are used in the plat, the lots must be referenced by both their block and lot numbering\. The block designations are often in a bolder or larger font than the lot numbers\.

title: Common Areas
text: Subdivision plats for residential subdivisions often designate certain tracts or parcels of land within the subdivision as __common areas__\. These common areas are typically reserved for parks, recreational areas and pools, boat docks, and water access or for future planned amenities\. Common areas of a residential subdivision plat are most often owned or controlled by a homeowner’s association for the benefit of all the residents on plat approval\. However, the developer may dedicate certain common areas for use by the public\.

title: Curve Table
text:
__Curve tables __provide information to properly mark the horizontal curves drawn on the plat\. Curves and arcs are common in a subdivision plat’s property boundaries, rights\-of\-way, and easements\. Each curve is labeled with a letter or number in the table that corresponds to a specific curve displayed on the plat\.
